title: Anthropic’s elaborate plan to keep Wall Street at bay
abstract: AI Policy Report Anthropic’s elaborate plan to keep Wall Street at bay Anthropic’s planned IPO raises questions over whether it can maintain its safe and responsible AI priorities. Anthropic’s planned IPO raises questions over whether it can maintain its safe and responsible AI priorities. by Robert Hart Oct 27, 2026, 4:51 PM UTC Anthropic cofounder and CEO Dario Amodei. Bloomberg via Getty Images Robert Hart is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes . Anthropic wants to have it both ways. With its impending IPO, it wants to tap the vast riches of the public markets and insists it doesn’t want to compromise its core mission of developing AI safely and for the benefit of humanity. But greater model capabilities bring greater risks, and shareholders eager for returns may have little patience for costly safety measures that slow products on their way to market. Sam Altman, the CEO of Anthropic’s archrival, OpenAI, has cited investor pressures as one reason the company is not pursuing an IPO this year. Anthropic hopes it can resist investor pressures with a mind-boggling governance structure. A “unique and complicated governance structure that has not been used before…creatively designed for this founder-led and mission-driven company.” University of Pennsylvania law professor Elizabeth Pollman told The Verge that Anthropic has proposed going public with a “unique and complicated governance structure that has not been used before” and that has been “creatively designed for this founder-led and mission-driven company.” Experts say it should give Anthropic freedom to pursue profits without letting shareholders force it to cut corners on safety or rush systems out before they’re adequately tested. But even the strongest legal protections can only go so far, and no corporate structure, no matter how well designed, can completely insulate a public company from the demands of the market. Foremost, Anthropic is a public benefit corporation. Simply put, it is legally required to focus on more than just maximizing shareholder returns, balancing these with its stated social mission and the interests of stakeholders, such as employees and specific communities. Patagonia and Kickstarter are among the better-known examples, with missions centered on environmental conservation and supporting creative communities, respectively. Another key safeguard aims to protect Anthropic’s mission by limiting shareholder influence over one of the biggest levers of corporate power: the company’s board of directors. Directors oversee the company and appoint its leadership, including the CEO. Directors can also hold executive roles, as is the case with Anthropic, with CEO Dario Amodei and president Daniela Amodei both sitting on the board. Shareholders typically have considerable sway over who sits on the board, giving them a means to replace directors or push for changes if they are unhappy with how the company is being run. For example, if shareholders are unhappy at what they perceive as unnecessary delays to market for optional safety testing, they may remove directors and replace them with ones more aligned with their interests, such as making money and being less cautious. “Anthropic is entirely insulated from profit seeking pressures, in the sense that ordinary shareholders have no ability to select the board or make business decisions.” Under Anthropic’s proposed governance structure, ordinary shareholders won’t have much of a say over who is on the board at all. Instead, four of the board’s seven directors will be chosen by a special body called the long-term benefit trust, explains Jens Dammann, a professor in business and commercial law at the University of Texas School of Law. It is a highly unusual setup for a major technology company. The trust is made up of “five financially disinterested voting trustees” with expertise in “AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise.” Through a special class of share called Class T stock, the trustees can appoint or remove directors in pursuit of their stated purpose: ensuring “that Anthropic responsibly balances the financial interests of stockholders with the interests of those affected by Anthropic’s conduct and our public benefit purpose.” The trust is designed to operate independently of the company’s commercial pressures, allowing it, in theory, to put Anthropic’s mission first. Ordinary shareholders technically have a say in the board’s three remaining seats. However, Anthropic has created another safeguard that keeps power firmly in the hands of its founders, called “Founder LLC,” which will control 50.1 percent of the voting power on shareholder matters. Given that many shareholder votes are decided by a simple majority, Founder LLC basically gives Anthropic’s founders the ability to block or force through decisions, regardless of how other shareholders vote. This means that they will effectively choose the remaining three directors, Columbia Law School professor Dorothy Lund told The Verg e. The prospectus says Founder LLC will “initially” be seven of Anthropic’s founders: Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah. “Our seven co-founders will initially be the sole members.” Notably absent is another cofounder, Ben Mann, who co-leads the company’s experimental Anthropic Labs arm, as reported by The San Francisco Standard . All in all, the arrangements would give Anthropic’s founders and the trust “tremendous power” over the company’s direction, shielding it from many of “the pressures associated with being a public company,” Dammann told The Verge . “Given the unusual governance structure Anthropic has chosen, I don’t see how going public, by itself, would undermine its ability to prioritize safety over commercial interests.” Ann Lipton, a professor at the University of Colorado Law School, agreed, telling The Verge that, legally speaking, “Anthropic is entirely insulated from profit seeking pressures, in the sense that ordinary shareholders have no ability to select the board or make business decisions.” But Lipton cautioned that the founders themselves have financial stakes in the company, which could influence their decisions. “Investors may not mind their lack of voice as long as things go well. But if things go sour, they may become quite frustrated.” And there’s a big difference between legal protections and immunity from market pressures. Anthropic, like all AI companies, “desperately needs capital,” Lipton said. “It’s not clear to me that any governance structure will protect against the market reality that unless Anthropic takes advantage of profit making opportunities at a faster pace than its competitors, it will not be able to fund its operations.” Lund expressed similar concerns. Anthropic will still “need to stay in the good graces of their investors,” she said, adding that “competitive pressure and capital needs can erode safety commitments over time.” Anthropic did not respond to The Verge ’s request for comment on whether it felt the company could actually resist shareholder pressure to massively accelerate AI at the cost of safety. Another potential vulnerability emerges if Anthropic’s founders start leaving. In its prospectus, the company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly its founders. Dario and Daniela are singled out as being especially “critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission. But beyond the loss of leadership, their departure could trigger significant changes in how the company is structured, potentially stripping away some of the safeguards preventing Anthropic from pursuing profit over safety. Under the proposed structure, Founder LLC would “sunset” if a majority of its members leave or the group chooses to dissolve it.

title: Firefox’s Smart Window adds AI form filling and webpage monitoring
abstract: AI News Tech Firefox’s Smart Window adds AI form filling and webpage monitoring An update to Firefox’s AI browsing experience can draw from your open tabs to help you fill out forms. An update to Firefox’s AI browsing experience can draw from your open tabs to help you fill out forms. by Emma Roth Oct 27, 2026, 4:14 PM UTC Image: Mozilla Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Mozilla is updating Smart Window — Firefox’s AI-powered browsing experience — with a new feature that can help you fill out online forms based on your open tabs. As an example, Mozilla says Smart Window can pull information from your online portfolio or LinkedIn page to paste your work history into a job application. You can try out this feature by clicking into a form with at least four text fields. From there, you’ll see an option to “Fill from sources,” which will show all of the tabs Firefox will draw from. You can then select or deselect tabs that you want Firefox to use, and the browser will generate suggestions based on the information in them. This feature currently supports text fields on web forms, but Mozilla is working to add support for dropdown menus and PDFs. Mozilla notes that data from your source pages is shared with Google’s Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, the AI model that generates the text suggestions. Along with this update, you can now ask Firefox’s Smart Window to watch a certain webpage for sales, new job listings, and other updates. You can set up a task by typing “/watch” in the Smart Window chat, describing what you’re looking for, and adding the webpages you want to watch. Firefox can then check for updates on a daily or weekly basis, but only when the browser is open. When Firefox detects the change you’re looking for, it will send you a notification through the Tasks button on the toolbar, or on your desktop (if you have desktop notifications enabled). Firefox will pause watching for updates if it doesn’t detect a change after 60 days, before stopping them completely after 90 days. Image: Mozilla These two features are rolling out to the Smart Window beta on desktop in the US and Canada. They’ll be available in other countries in the “coming months.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: Google’s next Genie AI model generates more realistic experiences
abstract: Tech AI News Google’s next Genie AI model generates more realistic experiences The Genie 4 world model offers more realism and can create audio to accompany its interactive worlds. The Genie 4 world model offers more realism and can create audio to accompany its interactive worlds. by Jay Peters Oct 27, 2026, 4:00 PM UTC Image: Google Jay Peters is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme. Google announced today its Genie 4 world model for generating interactive experiences using AI. The company says the model has four main updates: It allows for more realistic worlds, lets users update an experience in real time with a natural language prompt, can generate audio, and uses Gemini 3.8 Flash under the hood to help with its simulations. It also can create experiences that are about two minutes long, up from one minute for the previous Genie 3 model. Google is pitching Genie 4 as a tool that could be helpful for things like pre-visualization for filmmakers, prototyping game ideas, and making training scenarios for robots. But the company warns that, as simulations run longer, details and object permanence can shift over time. I haven’t been able to try Genie 4 for myself — it’s launching first as a “research preview” to “trusted testers” — so I can’t tell you how it compares to the Genie 3-powered Project Genie, which I used to generate bad Nintendo knockoffs . But here are some examples from Google demonstrating what’s possible with the new model. Genie 4 will be “coming soon” to Google AI Ultra subscribers, Google says, and the company has opened a waitlist where you can apply to be able to try it in Project Genie. title: Apple is adding an AI chatbot to Pages, Keynote, and Numbers
abstract: Tech AI News Apple is adding an AI chatbot to Pages, Keynote, and Numbers The new AI assistant can draft and restructure content in Pages, while organizing data in Numbers. The new AI assistant can draft and restructure content in Pages, while organizing data in Numbers. by Emma Roth Oct 27, 2026, 1:50 PM UTC Image: Apple Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Apple is bringing an AI assistant to its suite of productivity apps , including Keynote, Pages, and Numbers. The assistant, which is built on AI models from Apple and OpenAI, can understand a document’s context to perform tasks like designing, animating, and refining slides in Keynote. In Pages, Apple says the AI assistant can draft, restructure, and tweak written content. It can also calculate, visualize, and organize data in Numbers, while suggesting chart types and building custom tables. Apple now lets third-party AI agents plug into its suite of productivity apps. Image: Apple Keynote, Pages, and Numbers now support the Model Context Protocol on macOS 27 or later, allowing third-party AI agents to plug into the apps. The AI assistant is rolling out in beta to devices compatible with Apple Intelligence. It works on devices running iOS 27, iPadOS 27, or macOS 27 or later. Several other updates are coming to Apple’s creative apps as well, with Pixelmator Pro introducing a Generate Fill feature that allows you to edit part of an image by describing the changes you want to see. Apple says the tool “automatically matches the lighting, perspective, and texture of the surrounding environment so edits blend in.” Generate Fill in Pixelmator Pro uses AI to carry out changes based on a prompt. Image: Apple Meanwhile, Logic Pro for Mac and iPad is getting a Liquid Glass redesign, along with an AI assistant that Apple says can “set up a vocal track from a single prompt” and edit existing projects. There’s also a redesigned Browser on Mac that uses on-device AI to automatically analyze, classify, and tag added sounds. Apple is launching an update to Final Cut Pro, too, which brings templates, graphics, titles, and transitions directly into the app through MotionVFX. Apple is also building the Content Hub directly into Final Cut Pro, featuring a library of stock videos, photos, and backgrounds. The updates to Apple’s Creator’s Studio will be available to existing subscribers for free in November. title: Data center backlash is uniting America
abstract: Election 2026 Policy AI Science Data center backlash is uniting America Some midterm races come down to ‘people who hate data centers’ versus ‘people who hate them even more.’﻿ by Lauren Feiner Oct 27, 2026, 10:00 AM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Election 2026 Policy AI Science Data center backlash is uniting America Some midterm races come down to ‘people who hate data centers’ versus ‘people who hate them even more.’﻿ by Lauren Feiner Oct 27, 2026, 10:00 AM UTC Part Of All the latest updates on AI data centers see all updates Lauren Feiner is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform. If there’s one issue that seems to activate all kinds of voters in 2026, it’s data centers. The rapid buildout of these massive server storage facilities — and the infrastructure construction and expenses that come with them — has sparked local opposition in communities across the country and become a major issue in many congressional and gubernatorial campaigns. At the same time, tech money has been pouring into many of these races. Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by venture capitalist Marc Andreessen and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, has already spent $45 million in a year. And Public First Action, an Anthropic-backed group that says it supports AI safeguards, says it’s raised $80 million . Both have funded Democratic and Republican-aligned groups. Other super PACs see an opportunity to push for stricter AI policies , like the recently created Tomorrow Together, which launched $4 million in ads for battleground House races, with messages about data center development and AI safety . All sorts of candidates appear to be distancing themselves from data centers and taking steps to assuage voters’ concerns about unconstrained buildouts in their backyards. How far they’re willing to go — including by backing an outright moratorium on development — varies. While many Democratic candidates seem likelier to back a pause, that’s not always the case. And though some Republicans have leaned on party messaging about putting development in local control, rather than supporting a ban, others say a pause is exactly what the moment calls for. Texas gubernatorial and Senate races Deep red Texas has the second-highest number of planned data center projects in the country after Virginia , and across multiple races, data centers have emerged as a key wedge issue. Democratic and Republican candidates are all trying to look tough on data centers but emphasize different messages in their plans. For example, in the Senate race, Democratic candidate and State Rep. James Talarico includes references to environmental impact and sharing corporate profit with the public, while Republican candidate and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton discusses the need to keep Chinese technology out of US data centers. Both, however, want data centers to bear their own energy infrastructure-related costs and want to do away with certain tax exemptions for them. In July, Talarico unveiled his “ Hold Data Centers Accountable Plan ,” which would end state sales tax incentives, give communities more of a say in data center development, require a closed-loop water system in new data centers to limit consumption, and create federal standards to protect the energy grid and environment. Talarico has also proposed an “AI Dividend” for Americans that would be funded by a tax on “AI-attributable profits.” For his part, Paxton’s “ Texas First Data Center Plan ,” unveiled in August, would support Gov. Greg Abbott’s state-level policies, including repealing sales tax exemptions for data centers, requiring them to pay for electricity they use and add to state capacity, and preventing AI data centers from building in rural parts of the state. On the federal level, Paxton says he would co-sponsor an existing bill making it easier for data centers to connect to off-grid power systems, introduce new legislation prohibiting the use of Chinese technology to power US data centers or infrastructure, and hold data center companies criminally liable if the facility “empowers AI chatbots that undermine children’s safety.” Talarico has also proposed an “AI Dividend” for Americans that would be funded by a tax on “AI-attributable profits” In the race for the governor’s office, Democratic challenger and State Rep. Gina Hinojosa has accused Abbott, the Republican incumbent, of “flip-flopping” on data centers. Abbott’s office put out a press release last year celebrating a $40 billion Google investment that would include three new data center campuses, but in August 2026, with campaign season heating up, he announced an audit that could slow new facilities connecting to the state energy grid. Hinojosa, who has recently called for a statewide moratorium on data center development, pounced on the perceived inconsistency. “Greg Abbott has zero credibility here. Nobody believes that the arsonist is about to put out the fire,” she said in a social media video. The outcome of these races remains highly uncertain. Cook Political Report changed its rating for the governor’s race earlier this month from a likely Republican win to one that leans Republican. It says the open field for the Senate race is a toss-up. Florida gubernatorial race In Florida, there’s a clash over whether large-scale data centers can be reined in with the right policies or if they should be outright barred in the state. Democratic candidate and former congressman David Jolly has pledged to install a one-year ban on hyperscale data centers on his first day in office, and hasn’t ruled out a permanent extension . In one ad , Jolly puts data centers in the same breath as crime in a list of things he doesn’t want in Florida. His Republican opponent, Congressman Byron Donalds, has previously supported data center development in the state and said Florida is “wide open” to build without destroying the state’s beauty. He’s more recently changed his tune though, and while he still doesn’t want to outright ban data centers, he’s tried to assure voters that he’d support policies protecting them from associated risks like higher energy costs. In July, Donalds introduced the Protecting Ratepayers Act , which would require data center developers to fund the energy and water needed to run their operations. He’s also supported a state law with some similar requirements and environmental guardrails. “In my Florida, if you don’t protect our pocketbooks and our people, you won’t build data centers, period,” he assures voters in one ad. Energy experts have warned, however, that Donalds’ pledge to lean on nuclear and natural gas could actually raise costs for consumers . Despite these efforts, he’s been branded as “ Data Center Donalds ” by opponents, and polling suggests he may have to fight for conservative voters who also strongly oppose data center development . An October NBC6/Telemundo Station Group poll found that 45 percent of likely voter respondents opposed data centers in Florida, with 38 percent in support and 17 percent undecided. A higher percentage opposed data centers in their own communities, at 59 percent. Still, the poll found Donalds has a lead of 48 percent to Jolly’s 41 percent, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percent. Ten percent of respondents were still undecided. Pennsylvania gubernatorial race In one of the country’s relatively few purple states, both candidates for governor have accused each other of changing their rhetoric on data centers just to get votes. Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and Republican challenger and state Treasurer Stacy Garrity each appear to have hardened their stances amid the widespread backlash to data center development, even though they previously touted opportunity in such projects.

title: OpenAI announces three big science discoveries and a new way to work with academics
abstract: AI News Science OpenAI announces three big science discoveries and a new way to work with academics This time OpenAI says it’s taking new advice from scientists on how to release the results. This time OpenAI says it’s taking new advice from scientists on how to release the results. by Richard Lawler Oct 26, 2026, 11:34 PM UTC Image: The Verge Part Of All the drama around AI’s takeover of mathematics see all updates Richard Lawler is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment. He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget. Less than a month after its mass release of hundreds of manuscripts that it said contained solutions to long-standing mathematics questions, OpenAI is back with three more “major” discoveries in math, computer science, and physics . What’s different this time is the choice to have external experts that OpenAI describes as “shepherds” guiding the results in computer science and physics, while for the math problem it says that they advised it to release the AI output for researchers to work through their own explanations. OpenAI results added to GitHub today: Local smoothing for the Euclidean wave equation. The proof uses an auxiliary partial differential equation to establish Sogge’s local smoothing for waves in every spatial dimension at least two. It also yields the Kakeya maximal and dimension conjectures and Stein’s spherical restriction estimates throughout the interior of the conjectured range. We are releasing the model output directly, as we did in our October 6 release. The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False. The paper gives a deterministic algorithm that exactly counts satisfying assignments of fixed-width CNF formulas in subexponential time and polynomial space. The case of 3-SAT refutes the Exponential Time Hypothesis. An independent working group of computer scientists led by Russell Impagliazzo, Ramamohan Paturi, and Ryan Williams will examine and explain the proof. At the group’s request, we are making the materials public immediately so others can examine them as well. This approach could have its own issues, the company admits, and the AGMAI panel of math advisers OpenAI put together just said yesterday that “we recommend that AI companies do not adopt” the practices of designating certain people to receive the output first, citing unequal access, borrowed reputation, and biased selection as a few of the issues. Instead, they recommended that in the future, AI labs release output on scholarly repositories, with Lean-formalized proofs, info on how the problems were chosen, funding for people working on understanding the results, and other information. The physics information has not been released in full, but is a “mathematically rigorous existence proof of certain interacting quantum field theories containing gauge fields and fermions in four dimensions, including Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and a unified completion of the Standard Model of particle physics.” According to OpenAI, “David Gross will lead a group including Michael Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor Klebanov, and Nikita Nekrasov that will shepherd this work.” The computer science collaboration is said to prove that the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) , which has been widely believed to be true, is actually false. OpenAI says verification of the result will be guided by a group of three experts that includes UC San Diego’s Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, who were part of the group that originally proposed it in 1999 , as well as MIT professor Ryan Williams . The group decided to release the AI output write-up and Lean proof on GitHub today . They also released an open letter to the community asking for input on how to examine the claim, and about setting norms for dealing with AI-generated breakthroughs: We would welcome discussion of three broader questions: What expectations should govern early access to AI-generated results, disclosure of conflicts of interest, and the use of unpublished material for subsequent research? How should credit recognize both new discoveries and the work of checking, fixing, simplifying, explaining, and extending them? How can we support students and researchers as methods and research directions change, while preserving the understanding and judgment needed to question results and develop new ideas? There’s similar documentation for the math breakthrough, where its model “produced a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in every dimension and therefore also resolve the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture in all dimensions.” Just a few months ago, NYU professor Hong Wang was awarded a prestigious Fields Medal by the International Mathematical Union for resolving the Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions. title: Anthropic is burning gas to feed the AI boom
abstract: AI Science Anthropic Anthropic is burning gas to feed the AI boom Anthropic is clear that data centers will run on gas, to the company’s own detriment. Anthropic is clear that data centers will run on gas, to the company’s own detriment. by Justine Calma Oct 26, 2026, 9:45 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge Part Of All the latest updates on AI data centers see all updates Justine Calma is a senior science reporter covering energy and the environment with more than a decade of experience. She is also the host of Hell or High Water: When Disaster Hits Home , a podcast from Vox Media and Audible Originals. As it prepares to go public , Anthropic’s S-1 filing makes generative AI’s methane dependency glaringly obvious. “Competition for access to electrical supply and data center locations with adequate power availability is intense.” In documents filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission Monday, Anthropic acknowledges that data centers are becoming increasingly reliant on “natural gas” — the fossil fuel industry’s marketing term for what is primarily methane — leaving the company’s AI data center buildout vulnerable to rising fuel costs and existing supply chain constraints. And in a possible catch-22, Anthropic admits that rising global temperatures — a symptom of burning fossil fuels — will increase the company’s operating costs. “Competition for access to electrical supply and data center locations with adequate power availability is intense,” Anthropic says, adding that some of its planned data centers rely on electricity generated by natural gas turbines on-site. Anthropic leases capacity from hyperscalers, but it announced a $50 billion dollar plan last year to expand data centers in Texas and New York. The US, the epicenter for data centers globally, is planning to build more fossil fuel generation capacity than it has in a decade as data centers demand more electricity. Donald Trump’s administration has sought to kill renewable energy projects while tilting the regulatory landscape in favor of fossil fuels , which Trump claims is a more important energy source for powering data centers around the clock than solar and wind farms that generate power intermittently. Now, a shortage of gas turbines is slowing data center construction . Some developers are installing gas engines on-site as a way to avoid long wait times to connect to power grids. Developers are also turning to more simple turbine technology at these sites as they face backlogs from turbine manufacturers, making on-site power generation less efficient and more polluting as a result. Data center electricity demand could wipe out decades of gains in air quality over the next five years, one recent Texas-based study found — raising levels of soot, smog-forming pollutants, and planet-heating carbon dioxide. Even as data centers create more greenhouse gas pollution, Anthropic’s S-1 points to climate change as a risk to its bottom line. It will have to pay more for electricity and water to cool servers at data centers as temperatures climb. Nevertheless, Anthropic expects increased competition for natural gas and pipeline capacity from hyperscalers and cloud service providers rushing to build their own data centers. “This competition could drive up the price of natural gas,” the company notes. Gas makes up the biggest chunk of the US electricity mix, 40 percent of the nation’s power generation . And Americans are already feeling the pain of rising costs as utilities scramble to upgrade energy infrastructure and meet rising power demand. Pissed-off residents have successfully blocked dozens of proposed data centers across the US . Anthropic acknowledges that the specter of ballooning utility bills is enough to interfere with a data center project. “If our efforts to secure electrical power are perceived to affect other utility customers and the broader grid, regulators may impose conditions, standby charges, or other requirements intended to address such impacts,” it says. If regulators push data center developers to shoulder more of the costs for new energy infrastructure, Anthropic says that could also raise its operating costs. And without a secure gas supply and the pipelines to transport the fuel, the company says, it might need to delay or abandon planned data center projects altogether. Ultimately, these challenges could stunt Anthropic’s growth: Any failure to secure access to adequate electrical power, any legal, regulatory, or other administrative action or change limiting the availability of electricity, or any significant increase in energy or compliance costs, could adversely affect our cost structure and limit our ability to scale our compute infrastructure, develop and deploy our models, and service our customers. title: Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3
Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel?
abstract: Back to Articles Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel? Enterprise Article Published October 27, 2026 Upvote 3 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai 📄 Paper | 📊 Data | 💻 Code Today we’re releasing Old Ideas, Novel Problems , a new study of how reliably large language models can evaluate the novelty of scientific research ideas. Alongside the paper, we’re publishing a benchmark, data, and code for testing novelty judges, plus an automated pipeline researchers can use to build new evaluation sets. At Ai2, we’ve been developing AI systems that support different parts of scientific discovery. DataVoyager helps researchers explore and analyze structured data, AutoDiscovery generates and tests hypotheses, and Theorizer synthesizes evidence across large bodies of literature into candidate scientific theories. Together with Asta , these projects point toward systems that can help researchers move from understanding prior work to proposing, testing, and refining new ideas. But generating research ideas is only part of the challenge of automating scientific discovery. Those ideas also need to contribute something genuinely new, which means these systems need a way to distinguish a novel direction from one that mostly repackages existing work. That judgment is often handed to another LLM—what we call a novelty judge . Novelty judges assess whether a research idea is new relative to prior work, either on its own or in comparison with another idea. There’s no standard way to build one; research teams choose a model, prompt, evaluation format, reasoning budget, and sometimes a literature-retrieval system. Those choices can materially affect the verdict. Yet these judges are often validated only on human-written papers rather than the AI-generated ideas they are actually meant to evaluate. Our new benchmark results suggest novelty evaluation itself is far from reliable. Across six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – seemingly small changes to the evaluation setup produce dramatically different judgments of the same ideas. In one experiment, changing just a few words in a prompt shifts a model’s accuracy in identifying which of two ideas is more novel by more than 50 percentage points. Retrieval and additional reasoning do not consistently improve judgments, and two purpose-built novelty evaluation systems perform worse than a simple prompted Claude Opus 4.6 baseline. If AI is going to play a larger role in scientific discovery, we need more dependable ways to tell whether it is actually proposing something new. Our work provides tools for studying that problem, while showing how much remains unresolved. Building a benchmark for novelty judges To test how reliably novelty judges can distinguish more novel research ideas from less novel ones, we first needed examples where there was strong evidence about the originality of the underlying scientific contribution. So we built an automated pipeline around ICLR 2026 peer reviews. Rather than treating paper acceptance as a proxy for novelty, we mined the reviews themselves for passages where reviewers explicitly discussed a contribution’s originality. That distinction is key; a paper can be accepted without being particularly novel as long as it is strong enough in other aspects. Likewise, a rejected paper with an original contribution can have other weaknesses. We created a high-novelty pool of 154 human-authored research ideas by selecting accepted papers in the top-rated 10% of their ICLR research area whose reviewers positively identified novelty and where no reviewer disputed it. We applied the reverse criteria to build a lower-novelty pool : 145 ideas from rejected papers in the bottom 10% whose reviewers raised originality concerns without any reviewer positively identifying novelty. In a separate check of the review-mining process, an annotator agreed with the extracted novelty-signal polarity in 47 of 50 cases; none of the disagreements would have changed whether a reviewer was counted as praising or disputing the paper’s novelty. Together, these two pools form our first evaluation setting, Human-Only , which tests whether novelty judges can tell apart human-authored ideas with strong evidence of higher or lower novelty. But in practice, novelty judges are increasingly being used to evaluate AI-generated ideas. So we created a second setting, Human+Generated . For this pool, we paired the same 154 validated human ideas with 154 ideas produced by a simple LLM generator. We assumed the generated ideas were less novel than their human-authored counterparts; these are weak labels, not verified judgments for every idea. The generator received only a research area and an instruction to propose a novel idea, with no literature search, tools, iteration, or feedback. This gave us a conservative comparison between ideas from a basic generator and contributions from top-10% ICLR papers whose reviewers had explicitly endorsed their originality. As additional checks, an expert independently reviewed 30 Human+Generated pairs, heavily weighted toward cases our strongest judge got wrong, and we rewrote the human- and AI-generated ideas into a common structure to test whether judges were simply reacting to differences in writing style. The expert preferred the human idea in all 30 pairs and judged none of the generated ideas novel. Importantly, many of our core findings don’t depend on the labels at all. If two reasonable evaluation setups give opposite answers for the same pair of ideas, that disagreement itself reveals instability. Small changes can produce very different verdicts Using our collections of human-authored and AI-generated research ideas, we tested how well six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – could evaluate novelty through both pointwise (i.e., absolute novelty ratings) and pairwise (i.e., comparing two ideas to find the most novel) comparisons. We varied one factor at a time: the prompt, reasoning budget, whether the judge could see related papers, how the ideas were formatted, how many judgments were combined into a final verdict, and – for AI-generated ideas – which model generated them. The largest shifts in performance came from how we prompted the model to judge novelty. For example, we showed GPT-5.4 the same Human+Generated pairs – each containing one validated human-authored idea and one AI-generated idea – with two prompts. One prompt told the model that reviewers had found exactly one idea in each pair to be novel and asked it to identify which one; the other simply asked which idea was novel. When we switched to the simpler prompt, accuracy dropped from 93.5% to 40.9% – below chance – and the model changed its verdict on more than half of the same pairs. By contrast, the same prompt change shifted accuracy by only about seven percentage points on the Human-Only dataset, which pairs human-authored ideas with stronger and weaker evidence of novelty. That suggests a novelty judge can appear relatively stable on human-authored research but behave very differently on AI-generated ideas. That said, human-authored ideas weren’t immune. We saw substantial shifts on the Human-Only dataset as well; the same change moved Claude Opus 4.6 accuracy by 21 points. The shifts were just less severe than on the AI-generated ideas. There was also no universally better prompt. For example, when judging ideas individually, dropping an instruction that warned judges not to treat trivial or incremental contributions as novel improved accuracy for some judges while reducing it for others. A prompt that works well for one model may not transfer to another, in other words. We also tested a common use of novelty judges: comparing ideas from two AI generators. We paired ideas from Claude Opus 4.5 with Claude Sonnet 4.5, and GPT-5.4 with GPT-5.1.

title: Mirendil Launches Fern 0.1, Its First Model, With 10M-Token Context
abstract: Mirendil has released Fern , its first AI model. Mirendil Fern is a from-scratch coding model with a context window of up to 10M tokens. Mirendil explains how that equals about 23 MB of code, or roughly half a million lines. That is a codebase on the scale of Megatron-LM, held in context at once. Fern 0.1 is the first version, built from Mirendil-Base after a short round of post-training. For developers, its like, you load a whole repo, a full training log or days of agent traces at once. Fern is a language model from Mirendil , an AI R&D lab. Fern is aimed at AI R&D work, not general chat. Mirendil lists 6 target uses: Fern sits on Mirendil-Base , which Mirendil says one researcher pretrained in 3.5 months. Total compute was under $10M, including experiments, agent token spend and data processing. AI agents wrote over 99% of the code. The researcher chose what to try and when to intervene. Training data came only from public sources: GitHub, public code, web pages and public datasets. Mirendil says it used no distillation, no synthetic data and no licensed data. The code was written from scratch on PyTorch and JAX. Fern is the smallest of 3 planned models. Mirendil-Base-Large (0.5 to 2T parameters) is over 80% through pretraining. Mirendil-Base-XL (2 to 10T) is over 20% through. Mirendil tested next-token prediction on its own repositories, concatenated into a 42.9 MB stream. It measured cross-entropy in bits per byte, where lower is better. Window sizes here are measured in bytes, not tokens. Fern’s loss fell from 0.246 at a 32K-byte window to 0.155 at 16M and 23M bytes. The other models were scored up to about 1M tokens, their advertised limit. At a 1M-byte window, Kimi-K3 scored 0.140 and Fern 0.165. So Fern is not the best predictor at equal context. Its advantage is that the curve keeps going past where others stop. RULER is a standard long-context benchmark. Mirendil ran 5 RULER tasks on Mirendil-Base, the pre-post-training model. It used greedy decoding, thinking off and exact string matching. Retrieval holds up well. Multi-hop reasoning drops to 45% at 10M. Each 10M cell uses only 20 examples, versus 100 elsewhere. Mirendil says broader long-context results are coming. Mirendil compared Fern 0.1 with open-weight and frontier models. Scores for other models come from model cards, leaderboards or Mirendil’s own runs. Fern 0.1 beats Inkling and Nemotron 3 Ultra on 4 of 5 tests. It ties Beam on SWE-Pro v2 Hard at 76.5. It trails Beam on SWE-Bench Verified, 73.4 versus 81.6. Every frontier and large open model in the table leads it. *Figures from Mirendil’s announcement charts. Check out the Fern announcement , the Mirendil-Base pretraining post , and request early access . title: vLLM Semantic Router Releases d3-ultra: A 27B Open Multimodal Decision Model
abstract: The vLLM Semantic Router team has released d3-ultra , a 27B multimodal decision model under Apache-2.0. The d3-ultra decision model does not generate text. It reads an input once and returns a probability for every answer to every question. For developers, that means routing, classification, visual grounding and video checks from 1 open-weight call. d3-ultra is a System One decision model from vLLM Semantic Router that answers typed questions with probabilities. It is the newest member of Decision 3.0 , a family that spans 0.6B to 27B. You send a state (text or JSON, plus images or videos) and a set of questions. Each question has a type: Images can also sit inside questions and options. A quiz can show a photo, then offer 4 etchings as answers. The core idea is state once . The model reads the input once per request and answers every question from that single read. The config shows a Qwen3.5-architecture backbone with 64 layers. 48 are linear-attention layers and 16 are full-attention layers. The card does not name its base checkpoint. vLLM’s recipe says the sibling d3 was trained from Qwen3.8-27B. Box answers always return exactly 1 box with a confidence. A confidence near 0 means the target is not in the picture. Questions over 131,072 tokens fail with max_length_exceeded ; nothing is silently truncated. The research team compares d3-ultra with GLiDE V1.2 , d1-ultra, d3-turbo, d3 and Jev 1.14 on 2 in-house tests. SR-Text has 10,411 text requests with 73,495 questions. Most recreate skills from 34 public benchmarks with new items. Another 4,896 questions come from 43 new task families, like SQL checks and ticket routing. Scores are chance-corrected: 0 is chance, 100 is perfect. d3-ultra leads every area except arts and human taste. There, d1-ultra scores 90.8 against 89.6, within the margin of error. SR-Box has 5,678 Box questions on 4,984 images across 10 domains. A box counts as correct at IoU 0.5 or higher. d3-ultra scores 58.2% over 10 domains and 54.6% over 9. d3-turbo scores 60.0% and 59.6%. Jev 1.14 scores 45.7% and 46.9%. The team says d3-turbo stays stronger on natural images, while d3-ultra leads on charts. Latency: on 1 AMD Instinct MI325X with AutoModel, 1 question about a photo takes 304 ms. 255 questions take 2.16 s, about 7.3 ms per extra question. Check out the model card , the GitHub repo , the Decision 3.0 collection and the Hugging Face Space . title: Baidu Open-Sources Unlimited OCR 2 for Hundred-Page Document Parsing
abstract: Baidu has released Unlimited OCR 2 , an open-source OCR model built for very long documents. The 3B model parses books, filings and reports of hundreds of pages in one request. Its core change is SR-SWA, a sparse attention scheme that keeps per-step decoding cost nearly flat. Weights ship under the MIT license , with code on GitHub . Unlimited OCR 2 is a 3B vision-language model from Baidu that turns ordered page images into structured text. Output covers text, tables, formulas, figures, headings and reading order. It succeeds Unlimited-OCR , released in June 2026 to push DeepSeek-OCR further. The config keeps a DeepSeek-OCR style layout. A SAM ViT-B plus CLIP-L encoder feeds a 12-layer mixture-of-experts decoder. Each token routes to 6 of 64 experts, plus 2 shared experts. The DeepSeek-OCR paper describes this decoder as DeepSeek3B-MoE-A570M. Baidu does not state an active count for version 2. In multi-page mode, each page costs 273 image tokens. Full attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length. During decoding, each new token scans a longer KV cache. At 273 image tokens per page, 100 pages add 27,300 input tokens before any output. SR-SWA stands for Sparse Reference Sliding Window Attention. It compresses text-visual attention into a fixed set of working references. Baidu’s model card gives 512 tokens as the example size. The config pairs a 128-token local window with top-16 selection over 32-token blocks. That is 16 blocks of 32 tokens, matching the 512-token budget. This keeps per-step latency and memory nearly constant as documents grow. It calls the result ‘unlimited-horizon’ parsing within a finite context window. Image encoding and total runtime still rise with page count. Baidu team tests on MPDocBench, with dozens of pages per document, and MarathonDocBench, with hundreds. MPDocBench-Parse is a public benchmark of 433 documents and 3,246 pages. We could not find a public MarathonDocBench release. Per Baidu’s leaderboard chart , Unlimited OCR 2 scores 84.6 on MPDocBench. Qwen3.8-Max follows at 78.3, then Qwen-3.8-Flash-Next at 77.4. On MarathonDocBench it scores 77.1. Kimi-K3 is next at 33.7, then Gemini-3.8-Flash at 28.6. The drop between benchmarks is the real story. Qwen3.8-Max falls from 78.3 to 22.9 on hundred-page documents. Unlimited OCR 2 falls 7.5 points. Its predecessor, Unlimited-OCR, scores 0.0 on MarathonDocBench. Sub-scores (MPDocBench / MarathonDocBench): Single-metric margins on MPDocBench are thin. Qwen3.8-Max scores 94.3 on text and 89.2 on formulas. All figures are self-reported and appear only in a chart image. Parameter counts and licenses from each model’s Hugging Face page. Benchmark scores from Baidu’s chart . The model card lists Transformers for quick tests and SGLang for serving. In Transformers, infer handles 1 page with dynamic tiling, called gundam mode. infer_multi parses every page of a document in 1 request, so the model keeps cross-page context. Loading requires trust_remote_code=True , which runs Python code from the repo. SGLang serving uses a customized wheel from Baidu, not upstream SGLang. Baidu’s example schedules 10 pages per window and reuses the previous window’s KV tail. Smaller windows cut peak memory but weaken cross-page merging. Baidu warns a default bias setting can trigger a 462 MiB allocation and run out of memory. Check out the model card , the technical report and the GitHub repo . title: OpenAI Launches GPT-6.1 Terra, Halving GPT-6.1 Sol’s API Price for Agent Work
abstract: OpenAI has released GPT-6.1 Terra , a fast model for visual reasoning, computer use and writing. It replaces GPT-5.6 Terra and is live in the API as gpt-6.1-terra . Standard pricing is $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens . For teams automating screens, forms and documents at volume, GPT-6.1 Terra changes the cost math. GPT-6.1 Terra is an OpenAI reasoning model built for high-volume visual and computer-use work. It accepts text and image input and returns text . The context window is 1,050,000 tokens, with up to 128,000 output tokens. Its knowledge cutoff is June 1, 2026. Reasoning effort runs from none to max , with medium as the default. Tool calling requires the Responses API. Supported tools include computer use, hosted shell, code interpreter, web search, file search and MCP. OpenAI’s listed use cases include matching product photos to catalog entries and interpreting technical drawings. OpenAI’s main influential test is Agents’ Last Exam v1 , a set of professional computer tasks. One task turns architectural drawings into a 3D model. At medium effort, Terra scores 57.6% at $0.29 per task. GPT-5.6 Terra scored 42.6% at $0.84 on the same setting. GPT-6 Astra also scores 57.6% at medium, but costs $4.82 per task. At max effort, Terra reaches 60.0% at $1.01 per task. Claude Opus 5.5 scores 63.2% at $8.82 per task on the same chart. OpenAI says Terra completes tasks over 3 times faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. On the OSWorld 2.1 offline set, Terra scores 66.7% at medium and 74.2% at max. GPT-5.6 Terra peaked at 57.1%. GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 78.0%, GPT-6 Astra 80.9% and Claude Sonnet 5.5 83.9%. On MMMU-Pro (Vision), Terra scores 85.5% at max effort. GPT-6.1 Sol scores 86.3% and GPT-6 Astra 86.7%. GPT-5.6 Terra topped out at 81.7%. Terra’s max-effort run costs $0.012 per task, against $0.065 for Astra. On OpenAI’s internal set of error-inducing prompts, the low-effort error rate fell from 53.6% to 16.7%. At max effort, it fell 18 points to 4.3%. The set is adversarial by design, so production error rates will differ. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Terra solves 50.3% at max effort, up from 21.5% for GPT-5.6 Terra. It still trails GPT-6.1 Sol (55.9%), GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (70.6%). OpenAI itself recommends Sol or Astra for the most complex coding tasks. On Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, Terra scores 58.3% at $4.15 per task. That beats GPT-6.1 Sol’s 57.0% at $5.47. Claude Opus 5.5 with fallbacks scores 63.3% at $23.21. Standard API pricing is $1 input, $0.05 cached input and $5 output per million tokens. Batch and Flex are 50% cheaper. Fast mode costs 2x Standard. Prompts above 272K input tokens bill at 2x input and 1.5x output. That is half of GPT-6.1 Sol’s $2/$10 and one-tenth of GPT-6 Astra’s $10/$50 . Claude Opus 5.5 lists at $4/$20. In ChatGPT, Terra is live for Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. Benchmark scores and per-task costs are read from OpenAI’s launch charts and are self-reported. Specs and prices come from each vendor’s model page. Claude prices: Anthropic pricing . Check out the OpenAI announcement , the API model page and the system card addendum . title: Google Gemini Omni: What It Actually Does, What It Costs, and How It Compares
abstract: Google Gemini Omni: What It Actually Does, What It Costs, and How It Compares Gemini Omni is a member of Google's Gemini generative model family, built specifically to create output from any combination of input types, starting with video. By Shittu Olumide , Technical Content Specialist on October 27, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence Someone generates a short AI video; it's almost right, except the jacket should be yellow instead of red. With most video generation tools, fixing that means writing a new prompt and hoping the rest of the shot survives the regeneration intact — the lighting, the framing, the way the character moved. That specific frustration, having to redo a whole scene to fix one detail, is the actual problem Google built Gemini Omni to solve, and it's worth understanding the real product before deciding whether it delivers on that promise. This is a straight look at what Gemini Omni is, when it actually shipped, what it can genuinely do, what it costs in real numbers, and where it holds up against the competition and where it doesn't. What Gemini Omni Actually Is Gemini Omni is the newest member of Google's Gemini generative model family, and per Google's own announcement , it's built specifically to create output from any combination of input types, starting with video. You can feed it images, audio, video, and text together, and it generates a video grounded in Gemini's broader reasoning rather than routing the request to a separate, disconnected media model bolted on the side. It's worth being precise about where this sits next to Google's other generative tools, since the names get confused easily. Nano Banana handles image generation and editing. Veo handles one-shot video generation from a prompt. Omni's actual differentiator isn't that it generates better-looking video than either of those — it's that it lets you keep editing a video through natural conversation, turn after turn, while the model holds onto what you established earlier: the characters, the physics, the scene itself. That's a genuinely different product category than "type a prompt, get a clip." The Release Timeline Google announced Gemini Omni at Google I/O 2026 on May 19, 2026 , in a post authored by Koray Kavukcuoglu, CTO of Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect at Google. The first model in the family, Gemini Omni Flash, rolled out the same day to consumers through the Gemini app and Google Flow for subscribers on the Google AI Plus, Pro, and Ultra tiers, and at no cost through YouTube Shorts and the YouTube Create app. Developer access came later. The Gemini API opened access to the model on June 30, 2026, still explicitly tagged as a preview release, under the model ID gemini-omni-flash-preview . The model reached general availability on August 27, 2026, as Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash , and that general availability release wasn't just a version-number bump — it bundled real feature upgrades: scene extension that now analyzes the last ten seconds of a clip for continuity instead of just the final second, extensions stackable up to a total of 40 seconds, a cheaper 360p draft mode for fast iteration, and improved style and character reference handling from uploaded clips. Anyone citing a single "Gemini Omni release date" is collapsing three genuinely distinct milestones into one, and the difference matters if you're trying to understand what was actually available when. Core Capabilities Native multimodality means the model processes text, image, audio, and video together as input, rather than handling each modality through a separate specialized path, which is what gives it more cohesive, consistent output than stitching several single-purpose tools together would produce. Conversational editing is the headline feature: every follow-up instruction builds on the last one, tracked through an interaction ID rather than requiring you to re-upload or re-describe the video each time, and characters, physics, and scene continuity are meant to hold across that whole editing session. World-knowledge grounding is Google's term for the model combining an intuitive sense of physics — gravity, fluid dynamics, momentum — with Gemini's broader knowledge of history, science, and cultural context, which is what lets it produce something closer to meaningful storytelling than pure photorealistic pattern-matching. On the generation side specifically, it supports straightforward text-to-video, image-to-video (turning a still photograph, sketch, or product shot into motion), and first-and-last-frame interpolation, where you supply a starting image and an ending image and the model animates a smooth transition between them. It also supports subject and style reference, letting you upload images or short video clips of a specific character, object, or visual style and have the model weave those into a new generated scene. And as of the August general availability release, video extension can add up to 40 seconds total onto an existing clip — generated by the model or uploaded — in successive 10-second increments. The Model Behind It It's worth naming the actual model identifiers rather than speaking vaguely about "the Omni model," since Google itself uses several names across its own documentation. The current, generally available model on the Gemini API is gemini-omni-1.1-flash . The original preview identifier, gemini-omni-flash-preview , still appears in Google Cloud's own model card for the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, where it's explicitly labelled a Generative AI Preview offering with its own separate terms. On that enterprise platform specifically, the model card lists a 131,072-token maximum input and a roughly 57,920-token maximum output — real technical ceilings worth knowing if you're planning a production integration rather than experimenting casually. Here's what's worth being honest about rather than guessing at: Google hasn't published a technical paper detailing Omni's exact underlying architecture, the way it has for some other model releases. What's confirmed is that it sits within the Gemini 3.x-era model family by both timing and Google's own positioning, sitting in Google's model documentation alongside Gemini 3.5 through 3.8 Flash variants. Beyond that, claims about its precise internal design would be speculation, and this article isn't going to pretend otherwise. How to Get Started There are three genuinely separate on-ramps here, serving different audiences, and it's worth being clear about which one actually fits your situation rather than defaulting to whichever is easiest to find. For everyday use, the Gemini app and Google Flow are the two consumer paths, both included in a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription , alongside a completely free path through YouTube Shorts and the YouTube Create app — no subscription required for that specific route. For developers, an API key from Google AI Studio and a short script against the Interactions API is the fastest path to testing it directly: from google import genai client = genai.Client() # A single text-to-video call against the current GA model interaction = client.interactions.create( model="gemini-omni-1.1-flash", input="A drone shot of a mountain landscape at sunrise." ) with open("sunrise.mp4", "wb") as f: f.write(interaction.output_video.data) client.interactions.create is the core call, and the model string is the one line that matters most to get right, since gemini-omni-1.1-flash is the current general availability identifier, while some existing tutorials and cached documentation still reference the older gemini-omni-flash-preview string from the June preview window. The response comes back as raw video bytes accessible through interaction.output_video.data , written directly to a file here, though for anything beyond a quick test, Google's documentation recommends URI-based delivery instead of inline bytes, to avoid hitting payload size limits on larger outputs.

title: Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude
abstract: Chapter 01 : Case studies Anthropic’s life sciences team is working to accelerate curing disease. Over the past several months, our scientists have engaged in deep research partnerships with six organizations developing new medicines: BigHat Biosciences , Bristol Myers Squibb , Divergence Labs , Enveda , Generate Biomedicines , and The Column Group . We've also begun drug discovery efforts of our own. In doing so, we've learned a lot about how Claude can support drug development, and how we’ll need to improve Claude further to realize AI's potential in medicine. We plan to scale this work up substantially from here . There are many opportunities to speed up drug development, even beyond the most commonly discussed applications of AI, like proposing initial designs for new molecules. Developing a drug involves many varied tasks: doing early research to identify a target for a drug and the right type of drug to engage it, designing a molecule with the right properties, optimizing it to be manufactured reliably at scale, drafting the regulatory filings needed to run clinical trials, designing and administering those trials, and much more. Our strategy to realize AI’s medical benefits is based on having AI increasingly involved in all of these tasks. There is no single problem to solve; the bottlenecks are distributed all throughout the drug development process. The best way to identify and work through these bottlenecks is to get deeply involved in real drug programs, across many different disease areas and stages of development. So, over the past several months, we’ve partnered with six organizations to do so. We’ve also started drug discovery efforts of our own, including programs for rare childhood forms of muscular dystrophy, where Claude handles much of the scientific and operational work. This work serves our goals in three ways. First, it lets us better understand the strengths and limitations of our models in relation to a much wider range of drug development tasks (we’ve already prioritized specific improvements to our models based on what we’ve learned so far). Second, these programs can serve as case studies for the wider life sciences community. If Claude is to significantly increase the rate of new cures, we need to work with many more biotechnology firms and integrate Claude more deeply into their development processes. Third, these projects should, if their positive trajectories continue, have direct impact themselves. We’re optimistic that some may result in effective new medicines for the diseases they target, including food allergies, rare childhood diseases, and several forms of cancer. In this post, we provide an update on our progress with our partners, along with technical reports and preprints that describe our thought process, methods, and early results in more detail. We then briefly outline where our work is headed next. Case studies Generate Biomedicines: modality engineering. Generate Biomedicines has been working on increasing the usefulness of a cancer treatment known as CAR T-cell therapy. This therapy has historically helped treat blood cell cancers; Generate aims to reengineer it so that it can treat solid tumor cancers too. To do this, they’re aiming to shorten one part of the therapy’s genetic instructions, which would create room for additional instructions suited to other kinds of cancer. Six Generate scientists used Claude Code to propose new designs for this part. One design was about 70% shorter than the standard version, and in lab tests it was more effective: it allowed immune cells to make roughly 10 times as many receptors (the proteins they use to spot cancer cells), it killed tumor cells more efficiently, and the immune cells remained active for longer. Read more , and see Generate’s technical report . Divergence Labs: hit generation. Divergence Labs is working on a novel way to treat food allergies. Food allergies are set off by a reaction from a molecule called IgE, some of which is attached to our immune cells and some of which floats freely in our blood. Divergence Labs is developing drugs that would detach the IgE from our immune cells entirely, rather than solely neutralizing the IgE circulating in our blood, as standard medications do. This could provide a much more effective treatment, but it requires a precise design, with two “arms”: one that would bind tightly to IgE, and another that would help prise IgE from the immune cell. Claude converted Divergence Labs’ goals into a detailed design plan, and then, largely autonomously, generated roughly 35,000 antibody designs in about a month to be narrowed down and tested. In those early tests, Divergence found “hits” for both arms: three designs that could bind to IgE, and 20 that could dislodge it. Three of those 20 appeared to dislodge IgE more than the standard medication. Its next step is to build a drug that combines the two arms. Read more , and see Divergence’s technical report . BigHat Biosciences: lead optimization. BigHat Biosciences pairs AI with an automated lab to improve potential drugs (or “leads”), which must bind their target tightly, remain stable through manufacturing and storage, and avoid clumping together (among other criteria). BigHat’s scientists and an Anthropic researcher worked with Claude to improve these three properties in two leads, both antibody fragments that could become parts of future drugs: one designed to target cancer cells, and one designed to keep a drug in the body longer. Claude, connected to BigHat’s lab data system, Reccy, proposed changes to each molecule, and BigHat’s lab made and tested about 1,010 variants in about 10 weeks. Partway through, the team suspected the standard heat-stability and clumping metrics were misleading. Claude and the researcher reanalyzed the raw data, then proposed different metrics and a protocol change to test them. BigHat’s scientists refined and ran it, and the main predictions held. Compared with the originals, the best versions bound more than 10x more tightly, the cancer-targeting lead stayed in solution 18°C higher, and the lead for longer-lasting drugs clumped more than 100x more slowly. Read more , and see BigHat’s technical report . Enveda: manufacturing and filings. To conduct clinical trials, companies need records showing that each batch of a new drug has been made to strict quality standards, and to submit an application to regulators, among other requirements. At Enveda, manufacturing chemists spent up to 75% of their time on paperwork. To ease the load, Enveda built a system that connects all of its manufacturing documents to Claude, then lets Claude flag any possible issues. Over tests on 1,061 pages of documentation, Claude caught all 11 issues that human reviewers had spotted—and flagged seven they’d missed. In the process, this method reduced human review time by 89%, from over 25 hours to less than three. Separately, Claude wrote the first drafts of two important regulatory documents. One took four hours, compared to about three months by hand. For the other, Enveda’s standard human review process found one minor error. Read more , and see Enveda’s technical report . The Column Group (TCG): company creation. Because drug discovery can be slow, expensive, and prone to failure, investors in biotechnology companies have favored safer, previously validated ideas over riskier new ones, even when the latter could help more patients. We’ve been working with TCG to see whether Claude can change this by cutting the time and cost of drug discovery so that investors can confidently support more ambitious ideas. Specifically, TCG is establishing Pleiades, a new company that will use Claude to run many more—and more complex—drug programs than is usual for a small team. This could be a model for how Claude can reduce both the scientific and the operational and administrative overhead required to run a biotechnology company.

title: How AI agents shape experts’ judgment calls
abstract: Chapter 01 : Study design Amaç Herdağdelen, Hailey Joren, Alex Tamkin When experts hand their work to an AI agent, the usual assumption is that they still make the decisions that matter. The agent writes the code, runs the numbers, and offers advice, but the expert decides what to measure, how to interpret ambiguous evidence, and what the next steps should be. Often there is more than one reasonable answer to these questions, and the decision will come down to the experience and values of whoever makes the call. We wanted to look at whether experts really do make those important decisions, or whether in practice they defer to their AI agents. In a study we report in a new paper , we asked 50 professional analysts to do a realistic statistical analysis with Claude Code. They all had experience in causal inference—that is, working out from data whether one thing causes another. Their task was to advise a farming cooperative on whether an advisory service it was running was effective and should be expanded. Along the way, the analysts had to make four choices between two reasonable options, such as whether to measure productivity as crop yield per hectare or as yield per unit of operating cost, and then make a final decision. To see whether they were making these calls themselves, we set up each analyst’s agent to favor one option on each decision, which the analysts weren’t told about. Which way the agents would “lean” would be decided by coin flip. The agent was told to make the best honest case for its lean, to change its mind if the evidence demanded it, and never to mislead. Across the four analytical choices, analysts went with their agent’s lean 86% of the time. If the agent’s input made no difference, we’d expect about 50%. When analysts had already expressed their own preference before the agent weighed in, they switched away from it 60% of the time if the agent disagreed, compared to 6% if it agreed. Afterward, when asked to explain their choices, 77% of analysts used the agents’ own arguments—sometimes word for word—but only 15% credited the agent as the source of those arguments. Analysts who followed the agents’ recommendations closely were about as confident in their final recommendation as the rest, and roughly as likely to call it the product of their own judgment. Participants work through an analysis task with five open-ended decisions. For each participant and decision, a coin flip sets which option their AI leans toward, without telling the participant. We compare how often participants choose option A under each lean. We don’t know how much this tells us about the real world. Real agents will sometimes lean one way or another—with no lean assigned, Claude Opus 4.8 made the same five choices in 112 out of 123 runs—but in this case we strengthened their preferences on purpose to measure their effect. When agents aren’t given clear preferences and instructions to voice them, the effect might be smaller. This isn’t a simple cautionary tale against working with AI. Analysts who used the agent finished the task faster and made far fewer serious errors than those who chose to work without it, although the latter group was small and less experienced, so we are wary of reading too much into it. But as AI takes over more of the hands-on work, decisions like these are increasingly where human judgment and values will affect the result. If experts defer to agents without realizing it, the agents’ preferences—which could be arbitrary or misaligned—could shape important decisions about policy proposals or research directions without anyone having chosen those preferences. This is particularly important for research into keeping AI safe. Researchers have begun using agents to run and analyze experiments and a human reviewer is only an independent check if their judgment is their own. Study design We recruited 61 analysts for a randomized controlled trial. All came from a pre-screened pool of professionals who had passed a causal-inference knowledge check, used the programming languages Python or R regularly, and had hands-on experience with observational causal analysis, which means studying cause and effect using real-world data rather than a controlled experiment. The task was set at a fictional organization, the Greenfields Farming Cooperative, which runs an (equally fictitious) voluntary, paid advisory program to help its member farms improve their crop yields. About 40% of members have enrolled. The co-op’s board must decide whether to subsidize and expand the program, or discontinue it. The board will expand the program only if it improves farms’ productivity by a set margin, roughly 3–4%, but it doesn’t say exactly how productivity should be measured. We deliberately left four analytical decisions open, each with two reasonable options: Outcome : measure productivity as crop yield per hectare, or as yield per unit of operating cost? Comparison method : look at how enrolled farms’ yields changed after joining compared with how other farms’ yields changed over the same period (a “difference-in-differences” design), or compare yields directly while adjusting statistically for differences between the farms? Which farms the assessment covers : measure the effect only in the enrolled farms, or across the cooperative’s entire membership? Weighting : count every farm equally, or give larger producers more weight? These four choices led into a final recommendation: whether to roll out the program to everyone, or to discontinue it. Analysts and agents could also propose a one-year extension. Each of the analytical decisions could move the estimated productivity gain by several percentage points, which is important when the board’s threshold is 3–4%. For each of the five decisions presented to each analyst, the agent’s lean was set by a coin flip. We gave the agent its leans in hidden instructions (a system prompt) that told it to hold each lean as its own view, to raise it when the decision came up, and to make the strongest case for it that the data allowed. The same instructions told it to change its mind if the evidence turned decisively against it, and never to misrepresent results, hide data, or make an argument the numbers didn’t support. Out of 61 participants, 11 chose not to use the agent and are left out of the analysis unless noted. Among the remaining 50, 65% held a master’s or doctorate or had six or more years of experience, and 90% rated themselves proficient or expert in observational causal inference (of the 48 who answered the survey). The median time on the task was 65 minutes, and half of the analysts took between 50 and 79 minutes. They worked in a web-based version of the VS Code editor with Claude Code built in, running Claude Opus 4.8 at High effort. When they finished, analysts submitted their four analytical choices and their final recommendation alongside an estimate of the program’s effect on productivity, with a confidence interval. They then completed a post-task survey. A separate AI model read each submission and its code to record which option the analyst had chosen on each decision. Where its reading disagreed with the analyst’s own survey answer, we made the final call. Results Analysts mostly went with their agents’ lean. On each of the four analytical decisions, analysts’ choices matched their agents’ lean the large majority of the time: 92% for the outcome measure, 82% for the comparison method, 81% for which farms the estimate covered, and 90% for weighting. Across all four combined, the result was 86%. Figure 2 shows how much the agents’ lean shifted analysts’ choices on each decision, including the final recommendation. Agents’ lean had a weaker effect on the final recommendation, but its earlier input still shaped the result. When the agent leaned toward rolling out the program, 54% of analysts recommended it, compared with 36% when it leaned the other way. (A one-year extension counts as not rolling out.

title: Manage costs and demonstrate ROI for Claude Code on Google Cloud
abstract: As organizations delegate more work to Claude Code, spend grows with it, and platform teams need a way to both control costs and understand impact. Inspired by a recent webinar (opens in new tab) with Google Cloud, we share how organizations using Claude Code can better track and optimize these considerations on Google Cloud, including three core levers: control, track, and prove. Controls for managing Claude Code spend Claude on Google Cloud has consumption-based pricing, so your bill is a readout of how much your developers are using Claude in your Google Cloud environment. Adoption drives usage; usage is what you pay for, and it’s also where the value shows up. Your Claude Code bill is a product of how many tokens tasks consume and the models that handle them. Token consumption scales with task complexity and conversation length. Chat is a Q&A conversation. An agentic tool like Claude Code spends more tokens per task relative to chat because it's doing multistep work: reading files, running tools, and reasoning across a whole task. Meanwhile each model has its own price per token, so matching the model to the task is the other major cost control. Visibility into the tokens and model choices impacting your organization’s bill each month is available through the Claude apps gateway and Google Cloud services. You can govern the spend and manage costs via three independent levers: Control . Creating guardrails that guide usage without over-restricting access and unintentionally blocking people. Track . Granular oversight of where the spend is happening, and where it will continue to go, before the bill arrives. Prove . Identifying the value your org is getting from spending these tokens and attributing exactly where it’s coming from. Here’s how to apply this control -> track -> prove framework to your own Claude Code on Google Cloud deployment. The governance toolbox Claude on Google Cloud comes with tools and capabilities for controlling, tracking, and proving the value of your spend. Google Cloud already gives you many native capabilities you can apply to tracking and controlling your Claude spend: Per-project billing . Allows you to host a dedicated project for Claude Code as a clean way to track costs. Billing budgets and alerts . Allows you to set budget alerts and get notified as actual spend crosses thresholds you define. Spend caps (Preview). Allows you to enforce a service-level Google Cloud spend budget with ability to manually lift the cap. BigQuery exports. Lets you analyze Claude spend alongside the rest of your cloud costs. Quotas. Claude models on Google Cloud have per-minute limits on requests, input tokens, and output tokens for each model family and endpoint location. Provisioned throughput.
