Pay a fixed fee for reserved capacity instead of pay-as-you-go. Claude Code and Claude apps gateway add their own tracking and control capabilities. The gateway is a self-hosted service, shipped in the same claude binary your developers already use, that runs in your Google Cloud project between Claude Code and Claude on Google Cloud. Developers sign in through your identity provider, such as Google Workspace, so every request carries a verified identity. That lets you set model allowlists per IdP group, and spend caps per user, IdP group, or organization, by day, week, or month. Here's how to choose and combine capabilities to manage the three levers measuring the cost and ROI behind your organization’s AI investments with Claude on Google Cloud: Lever 1: Control The control lever is all about providing guardrails that guide developers in their Claude Code use, instead of restricting them with arbitrary caps. Guiding rather than restricting is important because high cost sessions are not necessarily bad — in fact, they're often high value, especially in Claude Code. Those sessions are generally your power users that are at the forefront, using new workflows and getting a lot of value from Claude and getting a lot of work done. Waste tends to sit in the long middle of heavy spenders. For example, they're using Fable for a daily routine that Sonnet can easily handle. Or maybe they have forgotten some scheduled task they no longer care about, but it keeps on running automatically anyway. There are four features that give you the guardrails to guide your users instead of restricting them: Spend limits (opens in new tab) . The Claude apps gateway allows you to set spend caps per user, per IdP group, or organization-wide, by day, week, or month. Group and organization caps are per-developer defaults that each member inherits, not a shared pool. Threshold alerts. When used with Claude apps gateway, Claude Code on Google Cloud warns developers as they approach their cap, first past 75% and again past 95%. These are in-CLI warnings for developers, whereas Google Cloud Billing alerts are meant for admins. At the cap, the gateway returns 429 until the period resets or an admin raises the cap, and you can script cap increases through the gateway's admin API. Model defaults and allowlists. Specify which models are available, per IdP group, via the Claude apps gateway which enforces the allowlist server-side on every request. We have found that setting a model default works really well, because most people will stick to the model default; if they want to switch models, they usually are switching for a reason. You can use model defaults in addition to or instead of model allowlists. Gateway Admin API. The gateway serves an admin API for spend limits (opens in new tab) , so you can set and change caps programmatically, for example using a ticketing workflow. Combine these capabilities to control your overall bill, but remember that control is only the first lever. Price per token doesn't give you the full picture. The most important metric is the cost per task, which can be monitored and analyzed by tracking this usage. Lever 2: Track This lever is all about seeing where spend is going and how it’s being used. The good news is that you can track Claude Code usage, costs, and tool activity across your organization. Primary tracking strategies include: Usage and cost observability. Claude Code's OpenTelemetry metrics and events (opens in new tab) report usage and estimated cost, broken down by skill, plugin, agent, and MCP server. Send them over OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) to tools you already run, such as Google Cloud Monitoring, through an OpenTelemetry collector or relayed by the Claude apps gateway (for centralized OpenTelemetry config). End-user usage view. Developers see their own spend and get usage warnings right in Claude Code before they hit a limit. Data export to your existing systems. Google Cloud Billing exports to BigQuery let you filter to Claude SKUs by model and token type, putting Claude spend alongside the rest of your cloud and AI spend. OTel flows to your O11y stack, and the gateway Admin API can feed spend-limit status straight into your ticketing system. Claude Code, whether running on developer machines or on cloud workstations, can export OpenTelemetry once you enable it, including sessions, active time, lines of code, commits, pull requests, tokens and cost, broken down by user, team, and model. The most recent releases of Claude Code also break usage down by skill, plugin, agent, and MCP server so you can see not just overall Claude Code usage but also which of your org’s internal skills and plugins get adopted. With the Claude apps gateway, you don't need to configure each machine. Set a telemetry destination on the gateway, and it turns telemetry on for signed-in developers. It also tags every export with the developer's verified email and IdP groups from their sign-in, rather than values configured on the client-side. To attribute usage to your own cost centers and departments, set the OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES environment variable (for example, department=engineering,cost_center=eng-123).

title: Claude for Financial Advisors
abstract: Today we're releasing Claude for Financial Advisors, a suite of connectors and workflow skills designed to help with research, prep, and documentation tasks that occupy an advisor’s time and keep them from client-facing work. Time is scarce among financial advisors. A typical advisory practice spends only a sixth of its time in client meetings, according to Kitces research . The rest goes to work around those meetings, piecing together information across systems to prepare, plan, and document what was discussed. Meanwhile, over four in 10 American workers say they don't know who to go to for good financial or retirement planning advice, according to EBRI's 2026 Retirement Confidence Survey . Time an advisor saves on prep and paperwork can go to a current client or new household they don’t yet have capacity to serve. Claude for Financial Advisors includes: Connectors, which let Claude access the custodians, asset managers, and wealth technology providers advisors rely on most, so an advisor can work with a client’s information in one place. Skills, which use that information to help with specific tasks, like meeting prep, portfolio analysis, and compliance checks, always in service of the advisor's own judgment and style. Connectors to the tools advisors already use New connectors bring in the CRM, custodian, portfolio reporting, financial planning software, estate tools, and meeting capture that advisors rely on. Addepar brings investment intelligence into Claude, giving advisors governed access to portfolio data, analytics and workflows across public and private markets. BlackRock brings its portfolio construction expertise, model portfolios, and institutional analytics into Claude through Advisor Center, so advisors can deliver holistic advice across public and private markets. CAIS opens its alternative investment platform to advisors in Claude, so they can query fund data, review manager and fund performance, and see a client's public and private holdings together. Charles Schwab connects Claude to Schwab Advisor Services custodial data, including balances, positions, transactions, cost basis, alerts, and money-movement status, so advisors can review client information, see which clients need attention, and prepare for reviews. Conquest Planning brings its Strategic Advice Manager planning engine into Claude so advisors can create new client plans, review and apply strategies, update existing plans and prepare for client meetings all in one place. Envestnet lets advisors summarize Tamarac accounts and households in natural language, with a financial plan snapshot from MoneyGuide. FactSet brings multi-asset class content including funds and ETFs, news, company fundamentals, analyst estimates, and market data to Claude, so advisors can research the companies and securities in a client's portfolio. FINNY, the growth and prospecting platform, connects Claude to an advisor's campaign results by channel and sequence step, and lets advisors enrich prospect lists from their CRM, or upload new lists directly in Claude. Flourish connects Claude to financial advisors’ books of business, enabling them to work with client information, check rates, manage invitations, and prepare for client meetings, all within Claude. Franklin Templeton provides publicly approved fund and share-class information in Claude, including performance, fees, NAV, holdings, distributions, and fund documents, along with its published market and investment insights. iCapital brings a client's alternative investment holdings into Claude, enabling advisors to view NAV, commitments, unfunded capital, recent capital activity, and performance, while more easily connecting those insights to the client's broader portfolio. Invesco brings portfolio intelligence and practice management insights into Claude through its Invesco for Advisors connector. J.P. Morgan Asset Management (55ip) extends tax transition technology to Claude, so advisors can evaluate the tax impact of moving a client's holdings into a new portfolio. Jump , an AI platform for financial professionals, gives Claude client context (meetings, documents, tasks) and Jump-built skills that prepare next steps for the advisor’s review. MSCI brings its proprietary data and analytics into Claude, so wealth firms can assess investment options across public and private markets, monitor performance, and evaluate rebalancing opportunities. Nevis , the AI platform for wealth management, draws on client information from meetings, documents, and communications to support meeting prep and follow-up in Claude. Orion brings portfolio reporting and Redtail CRM insights into Claude for household reviews, opportunity analysis, meeting prep and follow-up . SS&C Black Diamond brings portfolio, performance, holdings and rebalancing data into Claude, so advisors can review their book, spot clients out of tolerance, surface tax loss harvesting opportunities, and generate client reports, tasks and rebalance sessions with their approval. Wealthbox connects Claude to client records and meeting history to power onboarding, meeting prep, and follow-up. Wealth.com gives Claude a structured view of each client's estate and tax picture, including trust and will summaries, tax return insights, and the full balance sheet, so advisors can begin planning with an organized summary of available information instead of documents spread across multiple systems. Vanguard brings information on its model portfolios and advisor investment solutions into Claude, so advisors can draw on Vanguard's trusted research, portfolio construction, and asset allocation expertise when making decisions for clients. Zocks , the AI meeting assistant for financial advisors, brings Claude the client intelligence it captures from every conversation, including profiles, goals, life events, and commitments. These join other connectors already available in Claude, including Microsoft 365, Salesforce, DocuSign, Box, S&P Global, Morningstar, and more. The Claude for Financial Advisors plugin, which bundles advisor skills and connectors into a single install, works with BlackRock, Charles Schwab, Addepar, Envestnet, iCapital, Orion, Wealthbox, Wealth.com and Zocks, and advisors choose which of these to connect during guided setup. Some partners also offer their own plugins: BlackRock is launching one for Advisor Center, joining existing plugins from S&P Global and LSEG. Skills built around an advisor’s day Each skill in the Claude for Financial Advisors plugin supports a specific moment in an advisor's day, from prepping for a client meeting to explaining a drifted portfolio, and routes to tools the firm already uses to run their business. Firms can adopt these skills as is from our Claude for financial advisors skill repository , or adapt them to their own workflows, service model and house style. Advisor onboarding connects a firm's tools and runs the first meeting prep automatically, helping a new advisor be productive on day one instead of week three. Alternative investments brief pulls a household's alternative investments from iCapital or Addepar into a meeting-ready summary, shown alongside the rest of the portfolio, instead of an advisor reconciling separate statements by hand. Compliance and AI policy highlights content that may warrant additional compliance review based on user-configured criteria, assists firms in documenting review workflows, and supports AI-governance documentation processes. Estate and tax brief checks a client's estate plan against actual account titling and beneficiaries, looks back at the prior year's taxes, and can create CRM follow-up tasks, so mismatches surface for the advisor to review. Portfolio rebalance review flags drift and concentrated positions against a client's target allocation, and creates a first draft explanation an advisor would otherwise write from scratch.

title: PrivacyLib: Privacy Controls at the Data Access Boundary
abstract: At Meta, many privacy requirements ultimately come down to the same question: Can we prove that a piece of data goes only where it is allowed? At Meta’s scale, rather than relying solely on manual privacy audits, which can go out of sync as systems change, we have developed Privacy Aware Infrastructure (PAI) to answer this question within the infrastructure itself. PAI offers efficient and reliable first-class privacy constructs embedded in Meta’s infrastructure so that products can keep evolving quickly. In previous posts, we have covered how data understanding , data lineage , and Policy Zones (our information flow control technology) play a role in PAI. Now, we are diving deep into PrivacyLib , a common library that runs inside the clients of hundreds of our data and processing systems at the point of data access. PrivacyLib plays an important role in the final stage of the broader PAI workflow: continuously enforcing and monitoring data flows. Before PrivacyLib, we integrated privacy enforcement separately into the clients of each data and processing system for each requirement. With this approach, implementing a new requirement across systems could take months. Each new requirement, whether purpose limitation or data flow discovery, needed the same set of capabilities: covering a wide range of systems; deploying in weeks rather than months; running on every data access without becoming a latency problem; and rolling out enforcement changes without taking the fleet down. Over time, this approach became harder to scale as requirements and systems evolved. PrivacyLib separates system integration from requirement implementation. We integrate each system once. When a requirement can be met at the point of data access, we implement it as a PrivacyLib module shared across the systems already integrated, so a new requirement no longer needs a separate implementation in each system. There are two kinds of modules: As internal AI agents became a new way of accessing data, we also added the Agent Observability module to observe agent-related data access events and help safeguard the data that agents can reach. Systems already integrated with PrivacyLib picked it up without new integration work, which is what integrating once buys: each new privacy capability arrives as a module, not as a project. PrivacyLib operates across a broad range of data access paths at Meta: Operating at this scale creates three engineering challenges: To illustrate how everything comes together at Meta’s scale, let’s walk through a privacy requirement that needs to be upheld when processing messaging metadata. Users exchange messages through apps like Messenger, which supports end-to-end encryption . As Messenger routes and delivers those messages, subject to applicable law, its backend systems process non-content messaging data (i.e., messaging metadata), such as information about when messages are sent or delivered, to improve product performance, detect abuse, and protect users from harmful conduct. A variety of these backend services use Logger, a client library that runs in the service process, to write this metadata to data warehouse tables. Before writing a record, the PrivacyLib integration inside Logger invokes Policy Zones, an enforcing module, to check whether the metadata may flow to the destination table. This check is broken down into two parts: what inputs need to be available to make a decision, and how the check is actually evaluated at runtime. After examining these two parts, we look at how PrivacyLib scales across systems and how changes roll out without disrupting the services in the path. Every Logger destination table has a LoggerConfig that describes the records written to it. MetadataTraceLoggerConfig defines one such configuration for message-delivery traces and marks it as containing messaging metadata: A logging destination can have many writers, so the annotation describing its output data belongs to the destination rather than to each service that writes to it. If every service declared the annotation separately, the declarations could disagree, or a new writer could omit it entirely. Declaring it once in LoggerConfig gives every writer the same description of the data. For this destination, MessagingTrafficMetadataPolicyTrait supplies the MESSAGING_TRAFFIC_METADATA table-level annotation, and annotateWithTableLevelPolicy () attaches it to the destination. LoggerConfig is Logger’s own schema, and each system describes its data in its own format. To give PrivacyLib a single form to consume, Logger’s code-generation pipeline translates the configuration into a PrivacyLib-compatible artifact. The generated MetadataTraceLoggerConfigPrivacyLibArtifact is derived from MetadataTraceLoggerConfig and carries the destination identity and the messaging annotation: The generated class above is used by Logger’s client in Hack , Meta’s typed PHP language. For its C++ and Python clients, Logger publishes destination identities and annotations to a central catalog. PrivacyLib uses that information to generate language-specific artifacts. In the C++ example in the next section, PrivacyLib uses the LoggerConfig name to load the C++ artifact for the destination. The artifact from the previous section describes one Logger destination. PrivacyLib also needs to know what a Logger write means and which modules should run. Logger’s Hack integration defines that once for all destinations: PrivacyLibOperation::write() declares PrivacyLib’s write operation for Logger, and enforcements() lists the modules that run on it. The Policy Zones module can affect the result, while the Telemetry Logging module records the evaluation without affecting it. Adding a module here requires no changes to individual destinations or Logger call sites. ZoneDataType::LOGGER tells Policy Zones that it is checking a Logger destination. In C++ services, Logger constructs the PrivacyLib request as follows: PrivacyLib uses configName to load the destination’s artifact. The hashed PolicyEnforcedLoggerWriteAPI::log value maps Logger’s API to PrivacyLib’s write operation. The remaining builder arguments identify Logger as the caller and provide the implementation that performs the write. dispatch() invokes the configured modules and records their outcomes. For the Policy Zones module, PrivacyLib provides the destination annotations from the generated artifact and the current processing context. For this example, Policy Zones evaluates two conditions: When enforcement is enabled, the Policy Zones module denies the write if either condition fails. PrivacyLib combines the results from enforcing modules into one response. A denial stops the write before Logger sends the record downstream. Observing modules emit telemetry without affecting the response. PrivacyLib enables privacy checks to scale across heterogeneous systems through a common execution model, lightweight evaluation and telemetry, and coverage for requests that bypass integrated clients. PrivacyLib’s integrations span systems with very different APIs: key-value stores, graph databases, ML pipelines, filesystems, and logging systems like Logger. Each integration maps its access points to one of five common operations, and PrivacyLib invokes its modules at each: Modules are written against these five operations rather than against each system’s native API. Reads, writes, and RPCs also have post-operation variants, so observing modules can run after the access decision has been made. Once a system provides the mapping, every compatible module can reuse it, which is why enabling an additional module on an already-integrated system takes only days. PrivacyLib runs inside the clients of data and processing systems because the clients already have the destination identity and request context that modules need. Keeping the evaluation in the same process avoids carrying those inputs across process boundaries on every access.

title: Memory-Enforced GPU Sharing in Kubernetes with NVIDIA CUDA 13.4
abstract:
Many AI workloads need only a fraction of a GPU. Giving each one an entire device can leave capacity idle; sharing GPUs lets platform teams serve more workloads with the infrastructure they already have. NVIDIA GPUs already support several approaches to sharing. Multi-instance GPU (MIG) splits a GPU into hardware-isolated instances that are transparent to the application, time-slicing lets several processes take turns without memory enforcement, and Multi-Process Service (MPS) lets them run concurrently in separate address spaces (sm-sharing). CUDA 13.4 now enforces a memory boundary that is transparent to the application with a new time-sharing mode, alongside the compute sharing mode (sm-sharing) that already existed in MPS. Here is what the CUDA release brings: An exact memory amount: A workload asks for a memory size and CUDA holds it there. An allocation above that size fails, just as it would on a smaller GPU. A range: A workload gets a guaranteed minimum plus a maximum it can grow into when memory is free. A compute mode: Each workload can choose to use its compute in an sm-sharing mode rather than using the default time-sharing mode. A transparent memory limit: Each workload sees only a fraction of the GPU memory. The missing piece: Getting there from Kubernetes CUDA provides the memory enforcement capability, but a Kubernetes cluster can’t use it on its own. On every GPU node, something has to: Run and supervise the daemons that these features depend on Apply each Pod container’s memory limits and compute mode before the process starts Report what each fraction actually uses, rather than what the whole GPU uses This work belongs on the node, independent of whichever scheduler placed the workload. GPU fractioning: An open-source Kubernetes operator A new open-source Kubernetes operator, gpu-fractioning , is hosted under the KAI Scheduler organization on GitHub. It runs next to the NVIDIA GPU Operator, which provides the driver and the container runtime setup. GPU Fractioning Operator handles three jobs: It sets up and runs MPS on every GPU node. It applies each workload’s memory limits and compute mode. It measures memory and compute use per fraction rather than per GPU. How schedulers pass GPU allocations to the operator The developers write the resource and mode annotations in the pod YAML. Then the scheduler selects the GPUs for a workload and records its memory allocation and compute-sharing mode in per-container Pod annotations. GPU Fractioning Operator reads those annotations and configures the assigned GPUs to apply the workload’s memory limits and compute mode: Annotation Meaning nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-memory.request Guaranteed GPU memory nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-memory.limit Maximum the container may grow into nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-compute.mode time-slicing (default) or sm-sharing nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpus.devices Which GPUs the container was assigned Table 1: Per-container Pod annotations that GPU Fractioning Operator reads to enforce a GPU fraction Any Kubernetes scheduler that can write these annotations can enforce GPU fractions with CUDA. The scheduler still has its own job: choosing a GPU with enough free memory and never mixing compute modes on one GPU. Using GPU Fractioning with KAI Scheduler KAI Scheduler is the first scheduler integrated with gpu-fractioning . Starting with v0.18.0, KAI Scheduler has a GPU-sharing mode called NvFractions . KAI Scheduler picks which slice of which GPU each workload gets and writes the annotations (see Table 1, above), and gpu-fractioning enforces them on the node. KAI Scheduler’s other sharing modes stay available, and administrators choose one per cluster. It can be enabled when KAI is installed: helm upgrade -i kai-scheduler oci://ghcr.io/kai-scheduler/kai-scheduler/kai-scheduler \ -n kai-scheduler --create-namespace \ --set global.nvFractions.set=true This also installs gpu-fractioning as a dependency. From then on, you describe a fractional workload with Pod annotations. There are four important annotations that answer four questions: 1. How much memory is needed 2. How far the workload may grow 3. How compute is shared 4. How many GPUs it spans How much memory: The request There are two ways to request memory: 1. As an absolute size: Use the per-container NVIDIA annotation and standard Kubernetes units: The container name ( app ) is part of the key, so it always targets the right container. 2. As a portion of a GPU by using KAI Scheduler’s existing annotation: gpu-fraction: "0.5" How far it may grow: The limit This ability is new in KAI Scheduler. A workload can declare a guaranteed minimum (the request) and a maximum it may burst into when memory is free. Which limit annotation you use depends on how you wrote the request: Request Type Annotation Example Absolute Size nvidia.com/container.<c>.gpu-memory.limit “80Gi” A Portion kai.scheduler/container.<c>.gpu-memory.portion.limit “0.8” Table 2 : Which limit annotation to use for each type of memory request The limit is optional. If it is omitted, the limit equals the request and the workload is capped at exactly what it asked for. A portion limit must be greater than the gpu-fraction and less than 1. How compute is shared: Time sharing or sm-sharing Figure 1. Time-slicing divides the GPU’s time. SM-sharing divides its streaming multiprocessors (sm) Compute can now be divided. Call n the number of workloads sharing a GPU: either way each gets roughly 1/n of the compute, and what differs is whether they take turns or run together. Time-slicing is serial: Workloads take turns on the whole GPU, and when every one of them uses its full slice each gets about 1/n of the time. Time left unused by one workload is shared equally between the others. This is the default. Each workload runs in its own error domain, i.e. full error isolation. SM-sharing is parallel: The GPU’s streaming multiprocessors (SMs) are split between workloads and all run at once, continuously. Nothing is carved out in advance. The GPU hardware allocates and releases SMs as workloads need them. When every workload is busy the split settles at roughly 1/n; when one goes quiet its SMs go to the others, and a single active workload can use them all. In this mode, workloads share a single error domain. Compute mode is now explicit and can be set per container: nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "sm-sharing" # or "time-slicing" A shared GPU runs one compute mode at a time, so KAI Scheduler never places a time-slicing workload and an sm-sharing workload on the same GPU. KAI Scheduler tracks this per GPU, not per node, so one node can host both modes on different GPUs. How many GPUs are utilized To get fractional capacity on several devices, add: gpu-fraction-num-devices: "4" The request applies to each device. A 40Gi request with four devices gets 40Gi on each of four GPUs. Putting it together: Examples of GPU fractioning An absolute size with room to burst on four GPUs with SM-sharing: apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: name: inference labels: kai.scheduler/queue: default-queue annotations: nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-memory.request: "40Gi" nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-memory.limit: "60Gi" # optional nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "sm-sharing" # optional, default time-slicing gpu-fraction-num-devices: "4" # optional, default 1
spec: schedulerName: kai-scheduler containers: - name: app image: nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:13.0.2-base-ubuntu24.04 This is an inference server split across four GPUs that needs a guaranteed 40Gi on each GPU, can use up to 60Gi when neighbors are idle, and runs alongside other workloads instead of waiting its turn. SM-sharing puts the workloads in one error domain, so use it for workloads you trust to run together. Half a GPU that may grow to 80% on two GPUs with time slicing (default): metadata: annotations: gpu-fraction: "0.5" gpu-fraction.limit: "0.8" # optional nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.

title: NVIDIA RTX Spark Powers Neural Rendering and AI Characters in Games
abstract: NVIDIA RTX Spark is a new Windows PC platform for AI development, creation, and gaming in slim laptops and compact desktops. Powered by an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and NVIDIA Grace CPU, it combines up to 128 GB of unified memory with the full NVIDIA CUDA stack and RTX technologies including ray tracing and DLSS 5. This post covers the following technologies for game developers building on RTX Spark: DLSS suite of technologies that boost FPS and improve image quality NVIDIA ACE updates for responsive, on-device AI characters RTX Kit SDKs for neural rendering, geometry, and character rendering NVIDIA Nsight tools for optimizing and debugging native Arm64 and x64 applications NVIDIA RTX Branch of Unreal Engine 5.8 for integrating RTX technologies into your Unreal Engine projects MotionBricks update for human-character motion DLSS on RTX Spark RTX Spark benefits from the full suite of DLSS technologies in supported games, including Super Resolution, Ray Reconstruction, Dynamic Multi Frame Generation, and 3D-Guided Neural Rendering. DLSS Super Resolution reconstructs frames from a lower resolution input to improve performance. DLSS Ray Reconstruction generates additional pixels to enhance ray-traced scenes. DLSS Dynamic Multi Frame Generation can generate up to 5 additional frames per rendered frame, automatically adjusting the multiplier to maximize smoothness. The latest NVIDIA app beta also brings a faster Performance Mode (Preset C) for Frame Generation, with minor trade-offs in image quality. DLSS 5 brings 3D-Guided Neural Rendering to RTX Spark DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering is supported on NVIDIA RTX Spark, starting with NBA 2K27. An October model update runs 2x faster than the September version and halves GPU overhead while maintaining comparable visual fidelity. It also reduces VRAM use at 4K by 20%. The model will ship by default in future DLSS 5 games. For developers, DLSS 5 adds a final stage to the graphics pipeline that enhances lighting and material detail. The engine-rendered frame, including artist-designed geometry, textures, and lighting buffers, remains the foundation, while developer controls determine what can change. Avalanche Software has taken advantage of DLSS 5’s SDK controls to tune the integration to maintain the artistic intent and style of the game. Figure 1. Hogwarts Legacy with DLSS 5 off (left) and on (right) Read the full DLSS 5 update here . DLSS 4.5 Unreal Engine plugin The updated NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 plugin for Unreal Engine gives developers powerful tools for delivering sharper images and smoother gameplay. Its second-generation transformer model for Super Resolution improves image stability, anti-aliasing, and visual clarity, while Ray Reconstruction enhances ray-traced image quality. On supported GeForce RTX 50 Series and RTX PRO Blackwell GPUs, Dynamic Multi Frame Generation adapts the frame-generation multiplier as workloads change, with 6x Multi Frame Generation producing up to five additional frames per rendered frame. A key addition in plugin version 8.9.0 is official Windows on Arm (WoA) support for Unreal Engine 5.8. Native ARM64 binaries and support for building and packaging UE 5.8 applications give developers a supported path to bring DLSS-enabled projects to RTX Spark systems. Alongside updated Streamline and NGX components and fixes for UE 5.8 Frame Generation issues, this release expands the plugin’s platform reach and helps developers prepare their applications for RTX Spark. NVIDIA ACE introduces Nemotron 3.5 Bolt for on-device AI characters NVIDIA ACE is our technology suite for creating in-game AI agents that deliver next-generation gaming experiences, and we’ve shared two exciting showcases this year: PUBG rolled out AI teammates in a public beta powered by our first-generation Nemotron small language model (SLM). It helped new players land their first chicken dinners and generated viral clips across social media. Aniimo debuted our more efficient second-generation Nemotron SLM, turning standard in-game pets into responsive AI companions that react to your voice. Players can check in on their pets’ feelings or teach them new tricks, which will bring a new level of immersion when it releases in early 2027. More intelligence, less memory Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is now available. This model offers ~40% higher average quality against our prior model on relevant benchmarks and outputs up to ~80% fewer tokens vs peers. It is purpose-built to power richer, faster in-game character interactions, with strong conversational capability, autonomous multi-turn tool use, instruction adherence, and grounding to game state, all running locally on GeForce RTX and RTX Spark. Figure 2. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt has best-in-class response quality and time to first token Engineered for maximum intelligence and speed per GB of memory, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB enables responsive local experiences while preserving headroom for graphics rendering and local speech models. Key features include: Multi-turn tool use : Call application APIs to carry out tasks across a conversation, with integration guidance for asynchronous tool calls Conversational mode : Toggle to encourage concise, speech-ready responses for natural back-and-forth interactions. Configurable reasoning : Enable reasoning for complex requests or disable it for faster responses, with integration options to cap thinking to meet latency targets. 64k context : Accommodate conversation history, instructions, tool definitions, retrieved information and game state. Multilingual capability : Support for 35 languages, building on a base model pre-trained on more than 140 languages. Figure 3. Every NPC becomes an unscripted AI character. Here, the player asks Farkas: “Do you really trust the Jarl?” Get started with NVIDIA ACE Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is available to developers via the In-Game Inferencing (IGI) SDK . To test it in a game, check out SkyrimNET, an AI NPC modding platform by MinLL for The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim . SkyrimNET transforms every NPC into an unscripted, interactive character with personal memory, voice, and autonomy, enabling dynamic conversations and context-aware quests generated on the fly. The platform supports both cloud and local inference across multiple language models. Download the SkyrimNET Plugin: GitHub Repository Download the ARM-Supported Loader: Mod Organizer Release NVIDIA RTX Kit brings neural rendering SDKs to RTX Spark NVIDIA RTX Kit brings neural rendering, complex geometry, and realistic character rendering to game development. Eight RTX Kit technologies are published with support for RTX Spark: RTX Neural Texture Compression (NTC) : Uses AI to shrink texture storage while maintaining visual fidelity comparable to traditional block compression. RTX Texture Filtering : Uses stochastic texture sampling after shading to reduce artifacts and improve image quality, including for difficult volumes. RTX Neural Shaders : Lets developers train neural networks and run them within shaders for new asset compression and approximation techniques. RTX Mega Geometry : Speeds up bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) construction for cluster-based geometry, helping developers ray trace more triangles and improve performance in complex scenes. NVIDIA Real-Time Denoisers (NRD) : Provides denoisers for diffuse and specular lighting and shadows, producing cleaner images from low ray-per-pixel inputs. RTX Character Rendering : Provides tools for rendering strand-based hair and skin with path tracing, including subsurface scattering and Blackwell-accelerated hair primitives. RTX Global Illumination (RTXGI) : Provides several techniques for efficient indirect lighting for ray traced and path traced applications. Opacity Micro-Maps (OMM) : Used to accelerate ray tracing of high detail geometry by efficiently encoding the opacity states of micro-triangles and micro meshes.

title: Fine-Tuning NVIDIA Nemotron to Know Local Rules, Not Just Local Languages
abstract:
As AI adoption expands globally, people across languages and cultures are using it in more aspects of their daily lives. General-purpose language models serve as a powerful foundation, but they sometimes lack the local knowledge, cultural nuance, and precision a particular application needs. Post-training can adapt an open model to these needs. With suitable data and evaluation, it can improve accuracy and usefulness while supporting safer interactions with the model. This gives countries and industries greater control over how their agents reflect local priorities and serve the people who use them. NVIDIA built Nemotron-Personas-France with French AI startup Pleias, and Nemotron-Personas-Belgium with Pleias and Belgian university KU Leuven. Both are part of the open NVIDIA Nemotron data program, which includes locale-grounded persona datasets for 12 countries that developers can use to adapt open models market by market. In this blog, we will discuss how to take Nemotron open models and post-train them with Nemotron datasets to tailor them for regional languages and cultures. Video 1. Demonstration of the process of fine-tuning Nemotron 3.5 Lightning using Nemotron datasets, recipes, and playbooks The difference post-training makes Let’s say you are developing an agent for the passport agency in France and the agent gets a customer question like this: Je ne peux plus me déplacer à cause de ma santé. Comment faire ma demande de passeport? (Translation: I can no longer travel because of my health. How do I apply for my passport?) A typical answer while running a foundation model with no post-training may look like this: […] Si vous êtes dans l’incapacité de vous déplacer, vous pouvez faire votre demande par courrier. […] Adressez le dossier complet par lettre recommandée avec accusé de réception à la direction générale des finances publiques […] (Translation: […] If you cannot travel, you can apply by post. […] Send the complete file by registered letter with acknowledgement of receipt to the public finances department […]) The response is unspecific, unsupported, and conflicts with actual documentation available on government web pages. For this kind of documentation, a government official must make a home visit for your paperwork—submission by mail is not an option. To improve an interaction like this, NVIDIA has released the Nemotron-Personas datasets for France and Belgium . Each persona is a synthetic resident grounded in regional demographic, geographic, linguistic, and cultural distributions. A generic persona reads like “a French adult who needs a passport.” A grounded persona has an age, a commune, a job, and a household that follow French census data, plus written profiles of the person’s work and daily life. That shapes what the person asks and how they ask it. It can also change the right answer: For a resident of French Guiana, the passport stamp costs €43, against €86 in mainland France. This walkthrough uses France as the example, but the same loop applies to any Nemotron-Personas market. Swap in another released persona dataset, such as Nemotron-Personas-Belgium—which spans Dutch, French, German, and English—update the behavior contract and reviewers, and the rest of the workflow stays the same. These datasets can be used to generate synthetic conversations for post-training that cover more of the people the agent will serve for better comprehension. The facts in each answer come from official procedure text, which the workflow pairs with each persona. The response in the interaction above after fine-tuning may look more like: Si vous ne pouvez pas vous déplacer en raison de votre état de santé, vous pouvez demander qu’un agent se déplace à votre domicile. Pour cela, vous devez fournir un certificat médical de moins de 3 mois attestant de votre impossibilité de vous déplacer. Vous pouvez effectuer cette démarche en ligne via le site de l’ANTS ou en vous rendant dans une mairie équipée d’une station d’enregistrement. N’oubliez pas d’apporter vos documents originaux (pièce d’identité, photo, justificatif de domicile) et de régler les frais de timbre fiscal. (Translation: If you cannot travel because of your health, you can ask for an agent to come to your home. For this you must provide a medical certificate less than 3 months old stating that you cannot travel. You can do this online through the ANTS site or by going to a town hall equipped with a registration station. Remember to bring your original documents (ID, photo, proof of address) and to pay the tax stamp.) The answer is much more concise, in character as a support agent, and focused on getting the details needed to resolve the issue, which is how a real customer-service reply reads. The following workflow will let you adapt a model to this task. When to use this workflow Use this workflow to adapt a model that already has some capabilities in your target language for application-specific requirements, such as terminology, formality, response structure, or escalation rules. Post-training can help make these behaviors more consistent and reduce repeated instructions. Persona-guided synthetic data can expand coverage when suitable conversations are scarce, restricted, or missing important cases. Pleias, for example, uses three Nemotron-Personas datasets, including France and Belgium, in its work on Lamina. Lamina is a spine-care assistant from a Pleias partner. The personas turn a few real patient cases into varied training conversations. They also let Pleias test the assistant across patient profiles. As Pleias puts it: “ Better grounded data is what makes a small efficient regional-specific model viable .” Persona grounding here is about improving coverage and reducing blind spots in the training data, not a guarantee of fairness or proper representation. The workflow below connects these stages, from defining the desired behavior to evaluating the adapted model: Figure 1. The persona post-training workflow, from defining target behavior and generating training data to fine-tuning, serving, and evaluation. The Nemotron repo provides steps for data generation, training, and evaluation based on the NVIDIA NeMo open training stack. Each step is a reusable building block with defined inputs, outputs, and configuration options. The repo also provides a collection of agent skills (ex: customization using NVIDIA NeMo Automodel ) that helps coding agents assemble these steps into a workflow. Prerequisites You need: Python 3.11 through 3.13, uv, Git, Docker, NVIDIA Container Toolkit and access to the Nemotron repository . One NVIDIA DGX Station GB300 or one NVIDIA DGX Spark. However, this workflow can also be adapted to other NVIDIA GPU systems. Follow along with the repo here . Run this to install the Nemotron repository locally: git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Nemotron.git
cd Nemotron
git checkout v0.2.0
uv sync --extra data-sdg --extra evaluator
uv run nemotron steps --help To properly follow this tutorial, we will be using the folder called french-public-service-assistant located here: Nemotron/ <- repo root: run every command from here
└── use-case-examples/ └── french-public-service-assistant/ ├── config/ (sdg_data_designer.yaml, peft_automodel.yaml) ├── scripts/ (sample_personas.py, build_seeds.py, audit_and_split.py, compare_models.py) ├── sources/ (procedures.json) └── eval/ (test_prompts.jsonl) Step 1: Define the target behavior and freeze a holdout set Before generating training data, define what a good response should do. These requirements guide both data generation and review. Dimension Example requirement Audience – Who are we talking to? French adults with varying technical levels Task – What is it supposed to do? Answer questions about identity-document and vehicle-registration procedures (ID card, passport, proof of address, vehicle registration) Language – How should it sound? French, with a calm, respectful tone Grounding – What facts is it allowed to use?

title: 3 Ways to Boost MoE Inference on NVIDIA DGX Spark
abstract: Generating tokens faster starts with identifying what limits inference performance. In the batch-size-1 evaluation of Ling-3.0-flash from Inclusion AI on NVIDIA DGX Spark, profiling showed that decoding was memory-bound: reading model weights drove execution time. Two operations stood out—the mixture-of-experts (MoE) computation and the output-layer projection that produces scores across the model’s vocabulary. Those findings pointed to two ways to improve performance: reduce the weight traffic in each decode step and generate more tokens per verification round. This post examines three techniques that address those costs: Humming MXFP4 MoE kernels to improve execution of the routed-expert computation. Online FP8 quantization of the output layer, or LM head, to reduce its weight-read volume. Multi-token prediction (MTP) speculative decoding with NEXTN to draft and verify multiple tokens together. This post explains how each optimization works, measures its effect, and examines an integration issue that can make the combined configuration slower than the baseline. Ling-3.0-flash serves as the implementation example, with code and deployment instructions in the Ling cookbook . Model and baseline configuration The evaluation used Ling-3.0-flash-fp4, a mixture-of-experts model with 124 billion total parameters and 5.1 billion active parameters per token. The model has 42 layers: 35 Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) linear-attention layers and seven multi-head latent attention (MLA) layers. Each MoE layer routes each token to eight of 512 routed experts, alongside one shared expert. For agentic workflows, Ling-3.0-flash provides a native 256K-token context window, expandable to 1M tokens. Compared with the previous Ling flash model, it improves long-horizon task stability, tool-calling accuracy, and harness compatibility. Developers can enable reasoning for complex agent tasks or disable it for latency-sensitive interactions. Improved spatial understanding supports constructing physical-scene grids and reasoning about relative positions in coding tasks. The baseline followed the official cookbook’s W4A8 configuration: FlashInfer MXFP4 MoE kernels, NVIDIA CUTLASS dense GEMM, and the –enable-fp32-lm-head option. The LM head projects a hidden dimension of 2,560 to a vocabulary of 157,184 tokens. For standard MXFP4 deployment instructions, follow the MXFP4 deployment notebook . Optimization 1: Humming MXFP4 MoE backend The first optimization replaces the flashinfer_mxfp4 MoE execution backend with humming. Humming is an independent kernel library available through the humming-kernels pip package. Unlike the FlashInfer CUTLASS path, Humming uses NVIDIA CUDA Runtime Compilation (NVRTC) to generate and compile CUBINs at runtime for the actual M/N/K dimensions, data types, and GPU architecture. It caches compiled binaries in ~/.humming/cache. This specializes kernels for Ling-3.0-flash shapes, including its relatively narrow moe_intermediate_size of 768. It also compiles at a finer granularity: an individual kernel completes in seconds, whereas the FlashInfer CUTLASS path uses ninja to compile 97 targets and takes on the order of tens of minutes. Performance is reported as time per output token (TPOT) and decode throughput in tokens per second. Configuration TPOT Decode throughput Relative to baseline Baseline 27.71 ms 36.09 tok/s — + Humming MoE backend 25.35 ms 39.45 tok/s +9.3% Table 1. Effect of the Humming MoE backend on Ling-3.0-flash inference on NVIDIA DGX Spark, using a synthetic workload with 32K input tokens, 2K output tokens, and batch size 1 Optimization 2: Online FP8 LM head quantization In the checkpoint, the LM head is stored in BF16 and listed in modules_to_not_convert, so it is not quantized during loading. Its vocabulary GEMM is 157,184 × 2,560, and the entire weight block must be read for each generated token. Under a bandwidth bottleneck, it is therefore a high-value target for compression. The optimization applies a dynamic FP8 quantization configuration only when constructing the LM head. The rest of the model continues to load with the checkpoint’s FP8/MXFP4 configuration. Moving the LM-head weights from BF16 to FP8 halves the read volume for this layer. The configuration is enabled with SGLANG_ENABLE_FP8_LM_HEAD=1. This setting is mutually exclusive with the baseline –enable-fp32-lm-head option, which outputs logits in FP32 and uses a slower vocabulary-GEMM path. Configuration TPOT Decode throughput Relative to baseline Baseline 27.71 ms 36.09 tok/s — + Humming MoE backend 25.35 ms 39.45 tok/s +9.3% + Online FP8 LM head 22.76 ms 43.94 tok/s +21.7% Table 2. Cumulative effects of Humming and online FP8 LM-head quantization on NVIDIA DGX Spark, using a synthetic workload with 32K input tokens, 2K output tokens, and batch size 1. Adding FP8 increases decode throughput by 11.4% over Humming alone Optimization 3: MTP speculative decoding with NEXTN The first two optimizations reduce the cost of each decode step. Speculative decoding follows a different path: it reduces the number of decode steps. Ling-3.0-flash includes a NEXTN prediction layer (num_nextn_predict_layers: 1), which can be used directly as a draft model without additional training or downloads. The configuration uses three draft steps and a four-token verification window. In each round, the draft predicts three tokens in sequence, and the target verifies four positions at once, accepting the correct prefix. The benefit depends on two quantities: accept length, the average number of accepted tokens per round, and the verification-cost ratio, the cost of one verification step relative to a normal decode step. The measured ratio was approximately 2.26. The principal source of verification cost was not attention computation; at batch size 1, KV reads were small relative to weight reads. Instead, the cost came from MoE expert activation: a normal decode activates eight experts for one token, while verification processes four tokens and can activate up to 32 experts. Note: When online FP8 LM-head quantization and MTP are enabled together, the draft model must share the entire LM-head module with the target, rather than only its weight tensor. The original Ling NEXTN implementation didn’t expose this interface. Without it, the framework silently falls back: the draft receives FP8 weights but interprets them as BF16, accept length drops to 1.00, and throughput becomes lower than a configuration with no optimizations. Sharing the full LM-head module through this interface restores normal token acceptance. Follow the Ling cookbook to enable FP8 LM-head quantization and MTP together. Configuration TPOT Decode throughput Relative to baseline Baseline 27.71 ms 36.09 tok/s — + Humming MoE backend 25.35 ms 39.45 tok/s +9.3% + Online FP8 LM head 22.76 ms 43.94 tok/s +21.7% + MTP (NEXTN, steps=3 / topk=1 / draft_tokens=4) 9.72 ms 102.88 tok/s +185.1% Table 3. Cumulative effects of all three optimizations on NVIDIA DGX Spark, using a synthetic workload with 32K input tokens, 2K output tokens, and batch size 1. MTP accept length reaches 3.90 tokens per round; these synthetic results do not establish gains on other workloads End-to-end results on GSM8K The component-level results above use a synthetic 32K-input/2K-output workload. Synthetic workloads help isolate individual gains, but their repetitive outputs and simple sampling systematically overestimate speculative-decoding benefits. The evaluation also included a strict end-to-end comparison across all 1,319 GSM8K questions. The evaluation used five-shot prompting, with demonstrations from the training set and the complete test set for evaluation, temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, top_k 29, max_tokens 32,768, and chain-of-thought enabled. Apart from the three optimizations, both evaluations aligned all variables: sampling parameters, parser, five-shot protocol, random seed, and memory allocation.

title: AWS named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Contact Center as a Service
abstract: I’m proud to share that Amazon Web Services (AWS) has been named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Contact Center as a Service (CCaaS) for Amazon Connect for the fourth consecutive year. We believe this recognition reflects years of work pushing on what’s possible in customer experience. When we launched Amazon Connect Customer, we set out to evolve how businesses serve their customers: to make personalized, intelligent experiences possible without giving up efficiency, flexibility, or control. That belief still drives how we build today. Customer expectations have shifted. People expect you to recognize them, understand what they need, and stay consistent across every channel. They don’t want to repeat themselves. They don’t want to navigate disconnected systems to solve a simple problem. They want interactions that feel natural, relevant, and genuinely helpful. Meeting that takes more than traditional contact center technology, it takes a comprehensive solution that brings together customer context, AI, and the flexibility to adapt. That’s what we’re building with Amazon Connect Customer. Customer experience without compromise What matters most to your customers hasn’t changed: they want to be known, they want their problems fully resolved, and they want to trust you in the moments that matter. Read the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant to know why we are recognized. Experiences that start with knowing the customer. Connect Customer builds a living picture of every customer: who they are, what they’ve been through, what they need next. Every touchpoint draws on that intelligence. Your customer feels known before a single word is exchanged. That’s what personal actually looks like. Resolution that carries all the way through. Most of the industry is still optimizing for deflection: getting customers away from humans as fast as possible. We took a different path. Connect Customer is built for the hard things: the disputed claim, the renegotiated mortgage, the disrupted itinerary that needs real action and can’t go wrong. We carry those interactions all the way through to resolution, and we make them feel natural and personal. Generative and agentic AI push this further: understanding what a customer needs and acting on it. Every action is auditable. Humans step in when the moment calls for it. You get enterprise scale and the confidence that nothing slips through the cracks. The companies that win the next decade of customer experience won’t be the ones with the most channels or the fastest bot. They’ll be the ones whose customers feel known, whose problems actually get resolved, and whose trust is earned in the moments that matter most. Connect Customer exists to make that real for businesses of every size. I’m proud of the Connect Customer team for receiving this recognition for the fourth year in a row. Our engineers, product teams, partners, and customers shaped what we’ve built. This is a moment to celebrate how far we’ve come, and a signal of what’s ahead. Every customer is unique. Every interaction should reflect that.
