title: Unlocking Investment Insights Without Migrating Your Data: Lakehouse Federation
abstract: In today's enterprise landscape, data rarely sits in one place. Financial institutions, asset managers, and individual investors face a common challenge: their most sensitive data including portfolio holdings, trading positions, and client information often resides in on-premises databases behind corporate firewalls, in the cloud, or across both environments. That challenge is compounded by the fact that the third-party data they need for analysis, including market data, analyst estimates, and financial fundamentals increasingly lives in the cloud. Traditional approaches force an uncomfortable choice: copy sensitive data to the cloud, stand up brittle ETL pipelines, or give up on integrating the two altogether. What if you could just federate the on-premises source, subscribe to the third-party data on the cloud, and go straight from those two catalogs to a dashboard and a natural-language chat, with no pipeline, no materialized views, and no persisted objects in between? That's Databricks Lakehouse Federation at its simplest. Databricks Lakehouse Federation lets you create federated connections to external databases like SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Snowflake, and more, and query them directly from Databricks using standard SQL. The data stays exactly where it is. No copying. No syncing. No compliance headaches. Add a marketplace data share on top of it, and you have two catalogs sitting side by side in Unity Catalog - one federated, one shared, that a plain SQL query can join like they were any two ordinary tables. Let's walk through a concrete example. Imagine you're a wealth management firm with: Your goal: Build an investment dashboard that shows your projected earnings, identifies high-risk positions, and recommends actions, all without exposing your holdings data to the cloud. Setting up federation is straightforward through the Databricks UI. Navigate to Catalog → External Data → Connections and create a new connection to your on-premises database. The connection securely stores your credentials. Once the connection is established, create a foreign catalog that maps to your on-premises database. This makes your external tables appear as native Unity Catalog objects. After this step, your on-premises data appears as a catalog, but the data never leaves your SQL Server. Every query executes against the source in real time. The Databricks Marketplace provides instant access to FactSet's comprehensive financial data. Search for FactSet , review the available datasets, and request access. Once the provider approves your request, you can subscribe to the relevant datasets. After subscribing, the data is available as a shared catalog in your workspace, organized into schemas: These tables appear alongside your federated portfolio catalog in Unity Catalog. You can browse them, preview data, and check schemas, all without any ingestion or data copying. With both data sources accessible through Unity Catalog, an asset manager can open the SQL editor and write one query that spans both the federated holdings on one side, the FactSet marketplace tables on the other. To the SQL author they look like two ordinary tables in the same warehouse. There is no pipeline to author, no materialized view to schedule, and no gold layer to maintain. Every time the query runs it re-federates the on-premises source live and re-joins it against the marketplace share. The dashboard is powered by the same combined query inlined directly into each widget's dataset. No views are created and no tables are persisted. Every widget re-federates the source on each refresh. It instantly answers questions like: The final piece: a Genie agent wired directly to the same federated holdings and FactSet marketplace tables. Genie receives the join chain and data-quality filters in its instructions. It translates natural language into the same queries the dashboard runs. The result: democratized data access. Portfolio managers, financial advisors, and individual investors can all get answers without writing SQL, and without anyone materializing anything. Databricks Lakehouse Federation fundamentally changes the economics of hybrid data analytics. Instead of the expensive, risky, and time-consuming process of moving data to the cloud, or the equally burdensome process of building and maintaining pipelines on top of it, you can bring the compute to the data and let a single query drive everything downstream. In this example, the walkthrough built a complete investment analytics solution that: All without copying a single row of portfolio data to the cloud. The future of data analytics isn't about moving all your data to one place and it isn't about building elaborate pipelines to reshape it either. It's about querying data wherever it lives. While this blog used investment portfolios as the example, this pattern – federate sensitive first-party data, subscribe to cloud-based third-party data, and analyze without moving or copying anything – applies broadly. Healthcare organizations can join HIPAA-protected patient records with drug interaction databases for treatment recommendations.Manufacturing firms can federate on-premises IoT telemetry with cloud-based supply chain data. Retailers can combine in-store POS systems with third-party demographic datasets . The common thread: sensitive first-party data stays protected while enabling rich analytics with third-party data. title: From spot fixes to measured gains: improving document extraction accuracy with ai_extract and MLflow Prompt Registry
abstract: Document extraction often starts with a simple loop: spot an incorrect field, adjust the prompt or schema, rerun the document, and check the result. That approach becomes unreliable as fields and document formats multiply. A change may fix one field while introducing regressions elsewhere, work for one layout but fail on another, or appear better simply due to normal variation across LLM runs. We saw this on a recent project that extracted roughly 40 structured fields from partner-submitted order documents across dozens of PDF layouts. Reviewers corrected and approved extracted values before they moved downstream, giving us human-reviewed ground truth for evaluation. The challenge was not getting ai_extract to return the fields. It was improving extraction without degrading the system overall. For example, the revision field sometimes returned status terms such as ORIGINAL instead of a revision number or blank. A small schema change cut errors for that field roughly in half. But across every field, total extraction errors increased by 9%. The lesson was clear: improving one field does not necessarily improve the extraction system. The pipeline already had most of the pieces needed to evaluate changes systematically. Documents landed in object storage and flowed through a Lakeflow SDP pipeline using Auto Loader. Bronze parsed documents with ai_parse_document, Silver extracted structured fields with ai_extract, and Gold published results as a materialized view. Predictions synced to Lakebase, where a Databricks App let reviewers correct and approve fields, and Lakebase CDC returned those approvals to the lakehouse. Two pieces were missing from the feedback loop. Reviewer approvals were available, but they were not assembled into a reusable evaluation dataset. At the same time, prompts and schemas were embedded directly in pipeline code, so even a small change to extraction required a code deployment. We addressed both problems by building a workflow around three questions: What should we change? How should we version it? And what evidence is enough to promote it? This post covers three parts of that workflow: Together, these steps create a repeatable path from a proposed extraction change to production, with evidence that the change improves the system as a whole. The rest of this post walks through the practices we recommend and why each one matters. You don't have to implement all of them on your own. Genie Code for document processing builds the Lakeflow job (ai_parse_document, ai_classify, and ai_extract with citations and confidence scores) and automates the core of this workflow with an evaluation and hill-climbing loop : For example, you can ask Genie Code: "Evaluate the extraction against my labeled table and tell me which fields are weakest," followed by "Accuracy on the revision field could be higher. Iteratively improve the schema and instructions, re-run the evaluation, and show me the before and after." Understanding the fundamentals still matters. It helps you judge Genie Code's proposed changes, decide when a result is good enough to promote, and extend the workflow for production, for example by versioning prompts and schemas in MLflow Prompt Registry. Each section below explains a recommended practice and notes how Genie Code can handle it for you. ai_extract takes three inputs: the parsed document, a JSON schema, and optional global instructions. The schema and instructions serve different purposes: The result is a structured value with one entry for each schema field. You can access individual fields directly, for example: extracted:response.revision.value . Start with the schema structure. When a field has a closed set of valid values, use an enum constraint rather than listing the allowed values in the description. Use numeric types for numbers and integers, and use nested arrays or objects for repeated structures. Then use schema descriptions for rules that types alone cannot express, such as: KEY : Keeping field rules in the schema makes the extraction contract easier to inspect and prevents the global prompt from becoming a list of unrelated exceptions. Reserve the global prompt for rules that apply across the document, including: For example, if entity names are mistakenly extracted from boilerplate footers or third-party contact blocks, a FORBIDDEN-SOURCES instruction can tell the model to ignore those regions. A useful rule is: If the rule defines one field, put it in the schema. If it defines how to interpret the document, put it in the prompt. Automate it with Genie Code : The hill-climbing loop follows the same principle. Its proposed fixes most often sharpen a field description in the schema, and are shown as a diff for you to approve before they apply. Not every transformation needs an LLM. Handle casing, separator removal, zero-padding, and mappings such as TELEVISION to TV with SQL or another deterministic transformation when possible. KEY : Use the model to interpret the document; use code to normalize the output. Sometimes the instructions are clear, but the document is difficult to follow. Large schemas, repeated line items, complex tables, and multi-page layouts can make it hard to keep values aligned with the right rows. For these cases, ai_extract version 2.1 offers precision mode: Precision Mode brings frontier extraction capabilities for more demanding use cases. With the prompt and schema held constant, it tends to help most on repeated structures and reduces over-extraction (the model returning a value where the correct answer is blank). Diagnose the failure before changing the configuration: The approaches are complementary. In our testing, the schema rule corrected a field the model misunderstood, while precision mode improved extraction of fields from complex tables. When an extracted value is wrong, citations help show where the model found its answer: Citations provide field-level bounding boxes that can be mapped back to element spans in the source document. This helps distinguish between two different types of errors: These require different fixes. Extraction errors may call for a change to the schema or prompt. Labeling disagreements should be resolved by defining the expected convention in the reviewer guidelines. Confidence scores can also help prioritize human review: Use them as a ranking signal, such as reviewing low-confidence fields first, rather than as an automatic quality gate. A high-confidence result can still be wrong. In Genie Code : The extraction tasks Genie Code builds include citations and confidence scores. You can ask it to "Set confidence thresholds per field from the evaluation results and route low-confidence rows to review," and use the Document Parsing UI to visually debug parsing and extraction. Reduce the friction of hardcoding prompts and schemas in notebooks by managing them as configurable, reusable definitions outside the pipeline code. A small wording change requires a code deployment, previous versions are difficult to reconstruct, and there is no evidence that the new version is better than the old one. MLflow Prompt Registry lets you version those inputs separately from pipeline code. Version both the prompt and the schema: field descriptions influence extraction just as global instructions do. Version only the prompt, and half of your extraction logic is still traveling as an untracked code change. Beyond the Genie Code loop : Genie Code helps you find the right prompt and schema. When you take that configuration to production, versioning it lets you promote and roll back changes without a code deployment. A simple alias strategy might use: The pipeline then loads the active versions by alias: The resolved prompt and schema are then passed to ai_extract . When a candidate is approved, mlflow.genai.set_prompt_alias can move @prod to the new version. The pipeline resolves it on the next run without changing the pipeline code.

title: BigQuery to Databricks: A Strategic Framework
abstract: Many organizations support a range of data and analytics workloads on BigQuery today, but are exploring ways to bring BI, ETL, and multi-model AI workloads into a single governance and operating model. An open Lakehouse with a unified governance layer can help simplify operations, streamline compliance across data and AI, provide predictable performance as needs grow, and create a foundation for new AI-driven use cases. A successful migration requires more than copying tables. It demands a phased strategy: moving data into open formats on services like Google Cloud Storage, transforming logic thoughtfully, and validating results with automated tooling. This guide outlines a migration framework across three pillars – Process, Technology, and People – for navigating that transition with minimal disruption and measurable business impact. The Process pillar defines how you migrate. Success depends on choosing the right entry point and managing the transition period effectively. The migration journey runs in sequence: assess the estate, choose an entry point, migrate, validate in dual operation, then decommission. Assessment comes before everything else: you cannot pick the right entry point without knowing what you run today. Profile the BigQuery estate first — datasets, query history and slot consumption — to find which workloads drive cost, which dashboards are actually used, and which tables are never queried at all. Lakebridge , the open-source Databricks Labs migration toolkit, includes a BigQuery profiler that automates this discovery, so migration waves are planned around what is actually used rather than what merely exists. Whichever entry point you choose, migrate in waves, not in one big bang. A big-bang cutover concentrates all the risk in a single moment — and if anything breaks, so does trust in the whole program. Waves keep the blast radius small: rank workloads on two axes — value to the organization (how visible it is to leadership, how directly it touches revenue, how urgent the compliance deadline behind it is, how many people rely on it day to day) and migration complexity — and start where value is high and complexity is low. Each wave then delivers a visible business win, reconciles before the next starts, and leaves the team's playbook faster for the one after it. Reserve big bang for the rare small, low-risk estate where running two platforms costs more than it protects. Most organizations navigate a Dual Operation phase using Lakehouse Federation to "shadow" workloads for validation. The key to ROI is setting clear "success criteria" (e.g., 99.9% parity) to trigger the immediate decommissioning of legacy pipelines, eliminating the cost of running two platforms. Dual operation works in both directions, and the right bridge depends on your entry point. BI-first teams use Lakehouse Federation so Databricks can read BigQuery while dashboards move first. ETL-first teams flip it: move ingestion and transformation to Databricks, land curated tables in open formats, and let BigQuery keep serving existing dashboards and applications from that same single copy — no dual-write pipelines, no export jobs, no second copy to reconcile. Migrating in waves keeps this dual-operation window short and narrow: only the workloads in the current wave carry the cost of running on two platforms at once, so the bill for dual operation stays proportional to what's actually in flight, not the whole estate. Treat BigQuery-as-serving-layer as a transitional state rather than a destination: the external tables are read-only on BigQuery’s side and carry limitations such as manual schema refresh after schema changes, so plan the cutover of the serving layer onto Databricks Lakehouse as the closing step of the journey. Unity Catalog transforms governance from a hurdle into a strategic engine. It offers a seamless 3-tier mapping (Project → Catalog, Dataset → Schema, Table → Table) that replicates BigQuery permissions while adding automatic, end-to-end lineage and treating AI models as first-class citizens. The mapping goes deeper than the object hierarchy. Unity Catalog gives you the same fine-grained protection natively: row filters restrict access row by row, and column masks and tags handle column-level security — so protection travels with the data instead of being rebuilt from scratch. And one sequencing rule from the field: migrate permissions before data, so each wave's cutover changes where a table lives, never who can see it. The technical pillar focuses on moving data into open formats on services like Google Cloud Storage, migrating logic to Databricks SQL and Spark, and validating results. Migrating from BigQuery to Databricks involves three workstreams: Data Migration, Logic Migration, and Validation. Choose the path by volume and freshness. Bulk history moves fastest through BigQuery’s export to Parquet on Google Cloud Storage, usually the economical route at scale, and the export doubles as a frozen point-in-time copy that simplifies validation. Continuously updated tables are read through the Storage API connector or redirected at the source, and small, frequently changing datasets can stay queryable through federation until their wave arrives. Everything lands in open formats, ready for the medallion layers. Never hand-convert an estate. Three tiers cover it: rule-based transpilation (e.g. Lakebridge) for the bulk of routine SQL, LLM-assisted conversion for dialect quirks, and engineers reserved for the genuinely complex tail. Orchestration follows the same pattern: scheduled queries and Composer DAGs map to Lakeflow Jobs. Budget for validation as seriously as for the migration itself — in the field it often consumes comparable effort. Run it at three levels: completeness (row counts), consistency (schemas and types), and accuracy (aggregate reconciliation plus row-level hashing), automated with Lakebridge reconcile, which supports BigQuery as a native source. One field lesson: small built-in function differences between the two SQL dialects can break hash comparisons — investigate mismatches before assuming data loss. Parity here is what triggers decommissioning in the Process journey. The open foundation pays off before the migration even finishes. Because Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg are open formats, the tables you land on Google Cloud Storage are readable by more than Databricks: BigQuery reads Delta through BigLake external tables and Iceberg through Iceberg external tables, and catalog federation between Unity Catalog and BigQuery (currently in preview) lets both platforms govern and query the same tables without copying them. Storage is decoupled from the engine — one copy of data, many engines. That interoperability is not a side benefit; it is the capability behind the low-risk transition patterns described in the Process section. The third pillar provides the ultimate ROI of a migration: a more capable, unified workforce. Ending the handoff culture. In legacy stacks, the gap between SQL Analysts and Data Scientists creates silos. In Databricks, shared Notebooks allow the entire "squad" to live in the same workspace, reducing communication overhead. Building the new skillset. Genie acts as the bridge for SQL-heavy teams. Analysts can use natural language to generate Python or Spark code, turning traditional analysts into versatile data practitioners without a steep learning curve. Pair that day-to-day AI assist with structured training, Databricks Academy courses and role-based certifications, so the new skillset sticks organization-wide instead of depending on a few self-taught early adopters. Engineering rigor. Teams move from "writing queries" to "building data products" by adopting software engineering best practices like Unity Catalog, Git integration and CI/CD.

title: Unify your productivity and AI data with Lakeflow Connect
abstract: This is the second post in our series on how Lakeflow Connect brings fully managed data ingestion to every line of business. Following our deep dive into unifying marketing data , this post focuses on unlocking the enterprise knowledge trapped within your organization's productivity stack. We’ll explore how native connectors for wikis, project management tools, and AI foundation models give your downstream AI agents the complete business context they need. Lakeflow Connect provides a comprehensive suite of fully managed native connectors across SaaS applications, databases, and file sources that ingest your data directly into the Databricks Platform . Each connector can be set up via a point-and-click UI or a simple API. From there, your data is incrementally ingested as governed, managed tables in Unity Catalog , with no infrastructure for you to provision, manage, or scale. Prioritized by customer demand, Lakeflow Connect's ingestion connectors span every line of business, including Customer 360, Operations, Finance, and Productivity—the stack closest to day-to-day work. The average company's productivity stack is a sprawl of project trackers, wikis, document stores, inboxes, and AI tools, each holding only a slice of how work gets done. Getting that data out has historically required a patchwork of custom pipelines that are slow to build and painful to maintain. The bar is high enough that the most impactful use cases stay out of reach, for example: AI agents powered by your enterprise's internal knowledge or visibility into operational analytics. Lakeflow Connect resolves this by providing built-in connectors to ingest seamlessly from across the productivity stack: With this breadth of connectors, Lakeflow Connect becomes the ingestion engine that brings scattered productivity data into one governed foundation, without the integration bottlenecks that traditionally slow teams down. For example, Toyota Finance Australia , the financing arm of one of the world's largest automakers, uses Lakeflow Connect to bring its Jira data into Databricks as a fully managed, zero-maintenance pipeline. Similarly, Seguros SURA , uses the Monday.com connector to turn isolated task boards into governed, enterprise-ready insights.. VaxCare , a vaccine management company runs the largest primary-care vaccination network in the U.S., and uses Lakeflow Connect's Confluence connector to feed its internal knowledge base into Databricks and ground an AI agent in it. AI agents can provide instant, grounded answers from your company's collective knowledge without employees having to hunt across wikis, drives, and inboxes. But an agent is only as good as the data behind it, and most of that is unstructured. With Lakeflow Connect, this is not a problem; our connectors can land unstructured content like files, pages, and messages as governed tables in Unity Catalog. The exact data, and the format it arrives in, varies by source: Whatever the source, the content lands in Unity Catalog as a governed table, where you can begin to transform it for downstream AI use cases. Either way you end up with text you can index for retrieval and put behind an agent. For a deeper look at document processing, watch this on-demand session, Intelligent Document Processing with Lakeflow ; and for more on how to get started, read the downstream RAG guide . M3 Accounting , a leading provider of hospitality software, uses Lakeflow Connect's GitHub and SharePoint connectors to unify its engineering and product documentation into Databricks. As AI agents and generative tools spread across teams, so do the questions about the models powering them: what are we spending, who's using what, is it compliant? To help answer these, Lakeflow Connect provides connectors for the biggest foundation model providers: Concretely, this enables a single, unified view of how AI usage and adoption are trending within your organization, so you can measure and report the ROI of your AI investments to stakeholders. Lakeflow Connect’s depth of ecosystem coverage also extends to Atlassian—one of the most widely used suites in any engineering or product org: With both connectors, you get a complete picture of your Atlassian data, the delivery and the documentation that surrounds it, side by side. From there you can track launches, bottlenecks, and resolution times across projects. You can also build AI/BI dashboards, and ask Genie about any of it in natural language. For example, Digicert , a global leader in digital security, uses Lakeflow Connect’s Confluence connector to reliably power its internal AI Knowledge Assistants without the overhead of custom pipelines. Another customer, Orizon , a Brazilian healthcare technology company, uses Lakeflow Connect's Jira connector to feed its leadership dashboards. For a step-by-step setup and tuning guide for the Jira connector, see Unify Your Engineering Data: Jira Ingestion Best Practices . Because every connector lands its data as governed Delta tables in Unity Catalog , the productivity and AI data you ingest becomes part of the same foundation as the rest of your enterprise data. From there you can query it directly in Databricks Lakehouse alongside your other sources, ask questions of it in natural language with Genie One , and ground the agents you build with Agent Bricks in current company knowledge. And because governance, lineage, and access control all come from Unity Catalog, access stays consistent regardless of the team or tool from where the data originally came. TRegs , a financial technology platform for treasury, risk, and regulatory reporting, is already building on that foundation. Lakeflow Connect is actively rolling out new connectors across every line of business, with support for even more connectors coming soon! Try Lakeflow Connect for free now. Watch for the next post in this Lakeflow Connect blog series to keep learning how to bring all your enterprise data into Databricks and give your AI agents the full context they need. Which productivity tools does Lakeflow Connect connect to? Lakeflow Connect has managed connectors for Jira, Confluence, Monday.com, Smartsheet, Aha!, GitHub, Notion, Glean, SharePoint, Google Drive, Outlook and Gmail. It also has connectors for OpenAI and Anthropic. Each connector can be set up in a point-and-click UI or through an API. Check out the full list of SaaS connectors from Lakeflow Connect. Can Lakeflow Connect ingest unstructured files and email? Yes. The SharePoint and Google Drive connectors land each unstructured file as one row, with its raw bytes in a content column. The Outlook connector brings in email bodies as text, and the GitHub connector brings in repository text files. Everything lands as a governed table in Unity Catalog. How do I prepare ingested content for an AI agent? Text such as Confluence pages, email bodies and GitHub source files is ready to chunk and embed after light cleanup. Files that arrive as raw bytes are first turned into text with ai_parse_document . You can then index the text for retrieval and use it to ground an agent. To help get started, watch this on-demand session, Intelligent Document Processing with Lakeflow , or read the downstream RAG guide . What data do the OpenAI and Anthropic connectors bring in? The OpenAI connector brings in usage, costs, API keys, projects, users and audit logs, so you can attribute AI spend by team. The Anthropic connector brings in audit logs, users and roles, and the content of claude.ai chats and messages. Together they give you one view of how AI usage and adoption are trending. What can I build once Jira and Confluence data is in Databricks? You can track launches, bottlenecks and resolution times across projects, and build AI/BI dashboards on the results. Orizon, for example, brought over one million Jira tickets from 168 projects into Databricks to feed its leadership dashboards. Confluence pages can also ground internal knowledge assistants.

title: Modular quantum computing takes shape with l-couplers
abstract: Modular quantum computing takes shape with l-couplers IBM researchers achieve a critical advance for scaling quantum computers. Date 27 Oct 2026 Authors Ryan Mandelbaum Neereja Sundaresan Topics Systems Share this blog Was this blog post helpful? Yes No Key takeaways IBM researchers connected two IBM Quantum Nighthawk processors using four meter-scale l-couplers. The work achieved quantum state transfer fidelities of 99%, demonstrating reliable transmission of quantum information between processors. The new inter-chip connection design is compatible with IBM Quantum Nighthawk and can scale to IBM Quantum Starling and beyond. High-fidelity l-couplers provide a key building block for modular quantum computers. For the first time, superconducting quantum processors have been connected using multiple meter-scale quantum channels with an average quantum state transfer fidelity of 99%. This research demonstrates a critical milestone for scaling quantum computers into the era of fault tolerance. Previous work from IBM and other research outfits featured high-quality proof-of-concept demonstrations of quantum operations between connected modules. However, those approaches were not readily compatible with implementing multiple l-coupler connections between large superconducting qubit processors. Our recently published work introduces a new design for inter-chip connections that are compatible with IBM Quantum Nighthawk and can scale to the fault-tolerant IBM Quantum Starling computer and beyond. How will quantum computers scale beyond a single chip? Realizing the full potential of quantum computing requires us to scale to much larger quantum systems than exist today, a path that won't rely solely on building larger chips. Instead, we have determined that the future of quantum computing depends on many processors working together with information that can move between chips. Modular quantum computers therefore consist of individual quantum processors joined by meter-scale interconnects inside of modular cryogenics—dilution fridges that scale but share a cryogenic environment. For IBM superconducting quantum processors, we call these long-range interconnects l-couplers, versus on-chip c-couplers. Meanwhile, earlier this year, we debuted our new modular cryogenic platform for scaling quantum computers inside of which these connected processors will sit. Four aluminum l-couplers connect IBM quantum processor payloads inside a dilution refrigerator. The cables run between the front and rear payload assemblies to enable quantum information transfer between processors. (Credit: IBM) What does the l-coupler work demonstrate? A variety of previous papers from quantum hardware outfits in the industry have demonstrated a variety of connections between different quantum processors. However these methods are not compatible with how large-scale quantum processors are made and assembled. But now, we’re demonstrating reliable high-quality l-coupler connections capable of transmitting quantum information between quantum processors with low error rates. This is a critical component of the quantum computing architecture that truly unlocks scalability. With connected processors, we can run more powerful error correction codes and larger quantum algorithms across higher numbers of entangled qubits. IBM research scientists work on hardware used to test l-couplers between IBM Quantum Nighthawk processors. The system includes four l-couplers and custom hardware designed to enable l-coupler installation after processor payloads are mounted inside a cryostat. (Credit: IBM) Our l-couplers encompass all components required for inter-module quantum operation. This includes the aluminum coaxial cable connected to the associated components on the chip, the simplified “l-qubits” it connects to, the tunable-couplers that connect the l-qubits with the cables, and associated controllers. L-couplers are connected after the processors are mounted in the dilution refrigerator. This work specifically demonstrates the connection between two IBM Quantum Nighthawk R1 processors with four l-couplers, each one with an 80-centimeter cable, linking the two chips inside of a dilution fridge. While the experiment wired out only a subset of the qubits for development purposes, the processor chips themselves are full Nighthawk processors. We report l-coupler modes with internal quality factors of 940,000, where quality factor is a dimensionless number representing a systems ability to store energy—higher is better, and quality factors on the order of 10^6 are appropriate for transfer of superconducting quantum information. We benchmarked quantum state transfer fidelities of up to 99.3%, with an average fidelity of 99%. In other words, the quantum state is correctly transferred over the cable 99% of the time on average. Finally, we used distant CZ gates constructed by transferring states across the different modules, achieving a two-qubit gate fidelity of 94.75% averaged over the four links. This distant CZ gate allowed us to generate entangled states shared between the two modules, including demonstrating of using two L-couplers simultaneously to generate independent entangled states. Why is this paper important? or What does this work advance? Building a scalable, modular quantum computer requires high-fidelity links between individual processing units located within a cryogenic cell or between adjacent cryogenic cells. However, these links must be compatible with scaling toward multiple connections in order to extend this technology to larger enterprise-ready use cases. As far as we know, this is the first time that superconducting quantum processors have been connected using multiple quantum channels with an average quantum state transfer fidelity of 99%. This work establishes our technique for implementing l-couplers as a viable path forward for scaling quantum computers to the fault-tolerant regime. What's next? Our roadmap projects that quantum will scale at an accelerating pace. A major focus for our hardware will be implementing error correction codes which will require meter-scale couplers between neighboring chips. Therefore, we anticipate improving the yield and reproducibility of our l-couplers, reducing their error rates, and scaling to more l-couplers that can easily be plugged and unplugged between larger and more complex processors—as we build connected Nighthawks and work toward IBM Quantum Starling. We have room to improve all of the metrics reported in our recent paper, and are aware of the steps required to make those improvements. We will continue performing research and development as we work to integrate the couplers into a larger system running more advanced workloads. Our agile process for hardware development and quick cycles of learning continue to yield critical advances in the lab and translate them to production processes. All told, this work propels IBM further along our roadmap toward scalable, modular fault-tolerant quantum computing. Was this blog post helpful? title: IBM and Kaggle launch Java framework migration leaderboard
abstract: ScarfBench (Self-Contained Application Refactoring Benchmark) is an open IBM benchmark for evaluating whether coding agents can successfully migrate enterprise Java applications across frameworks while preserving working application behavior. Across Jakarta EE, Quarkus, and Spring migrations, it tests whether generated applications build, start, and continue to behave as expected, using both focused workloads and whole applications Modernizing an enterprise application is not a single-file coding task. Moving an application between frameworks can require coordinated changes to dependency injection, persistence, database access, web endpoints, build systems, framework descriptors, and deployment infrastructure. A coding agent can produce a migration that looks plausible, or even compiles, while the application still fails when deployed or exercised against its expected behavior. ScarfBench asks a practical question: Can an agent take an unfamiliar application, migrate it across framework boundaries, and leave behind software that still works? IBM introduced ScarfBench earlier in 2026 as a reproducible benchmark for AI-driven migrations. Now IBM and Kaggle are partnering to make that evaluation easier to reproduce, compare, and extend over time. Kaggle consulted on the evaluation design, independently reproduced and ran ScarfBench on its platform while sponsoring the compute, and will maintain the benchmark as new models are released. The collaboration turns ScarfBench from a published benchmark into a continuously updated view of progress in agentic software modernization. The original ScarfBench announcement described the benchmark design, developer-verified workloads, and reproducible evaluation approach in detail. This post focuses on what the latest evaluation tells us about model-and-agent-harness combinations, where they fail, and how the benchmark is evolving with Kaggle. Evaluating model-and-harness combinations ScarfBench evaluates an agentic system rather than a language model in isolation. Each result reflects a model paired with a coding-agent harness that determines how it interacts with the repository and development environment. The results should therefore be read as model/harness results, not as measurements of the underlying model alone. Across 204 migration tasks, Gemini 4 Argon with Antigravity ranked first on the primary smoke-test metric at 75.2%, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code at 70.5% and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code at 69.8%. Ten model-and-harness configurations were evaluated. Rank Model Harness Smoke % All pass % Mean % 1 Gemini 4 Argon Antigravity 75.2 71.1 85.9 2 Claude Opus 5.5 Claude Code 70.5 72.1 82.0 3 Claude Opus 5 Claude Code 69.8 60.8 79.7 4 GPT-6.1 Sol Codex 68.4 62.7 76.8 5 Gemini 3.8 Flash mini-swe 66.0 62.3 77.6 6 GPT-6 Astra Codex 65.4 61.4 75.4 7 Qwen 3.8 Max qwen-code 63.7 59.3 76.1 8 Kimi K3 kimi-code 61.1 50.7 71.2 9 Gemini 3.1 Pro OpenHands 39.5 35.1 50.5 10 Gemma 4 26B-A4B mini-swe 24.5 17.6 30.8 The three metrics reveal an important nuance. The smoke score, the leaderboard metric, awards partial credit and gives larger test suites more weight. On that measure, the Gemini 4 Argon + Antigravity combination had the strongest result. But Claude Opus 5.5 + Claude Code had the highest all-tests-pass rate at 72.1%, narrowly ahead of Gemini 4 Argon. In other words, the Argon/Antigravity combination earned the most partial credit across the benchmark, while the Opus 5.5/Claude Code combination converted slightly more individual migration tasks into completely green test suites. The ranking remains stable under a sensitivity analysis. Four of the 204 migration tasks received zero behavioral-test credit from every evaluated model/harness combination. Excluding those four tasks raised the absolute scores but did not change the ordering at the top: Gemini 4 Argon + Antigravity scored 79.4%, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 + Claude Code at 74.5% and Claude Opus 5 + Claude Code at 73.7%. This result suggests that the relative ranking is not driven by this small set of uniformly difficult tasks. Even the strongest combination leaves substantial headroom: The best overall smoke score was 75.2% across the full benchmark, and no configuration fully passed more than about three-quarters of the migrations. The biggest differentiator is behavioral fidelity, not compilation The clearest result is the gap between code that builds and software that behaves correctly. After excluding the four all-zero tasks, Claude Opus 5 + Claude Code, Gemini 4 Argon + Antigravity and Gemini 3.8 Flash + mini-swe each compiled 100% of tasks, GPT-6 Astra + Codex and Kimi K3 + kimi-code compiled 99.0% and 98.5%, and Claude Opus 5.5 + Claude Code and GPT-6.1 Sol + Codex compiled 98.0% and 98.5%. Yet smoke-test scores remained much lower. Across the 10 configurations, compile success among solvable tasks spanned about 25 percentage points, but most configurations cluster near the top, with 8 of 10 compiling 97% or more; smoke-test performance spanned more than 50 points. Among applications that successfully deployed, the leading configurations clustered at roughly 63 to 76% for fully passing tests; Kimi K3 + kimi-code fell to 53%, Gemini 3.1 Pro + OpenHands to 42%, and Gemma 4 26B-A4B + mini-swe to 26%. In this evaluation, preserving behavior was a much stronger discriminator than getting the migrated application to compile. Where agent configurations fail Of 745 classified failing runs, 535 (approximately 72%) were runtime behavioral failures: The application built and often booted but failed behavioral validation. This group included 304 content or assertion mismatches and 210 lost-route/404 failures; 21 were explicit HTTP 500/405 errors. Compile or packaging failures accounted for roughly 20% (152 runs), and boot or dependency-injection crashes for roughly 8% (58 runs). Lost routes and HTTP semantics: In concurrency-taskcreator-quarkus-to-jakarta, Claude Opus 5 + Claude Code scored 0/6 after /taskinfo returned “File not found” and a test expecting HTTP 405 failed. In address-book-jakarta-to-quarkus, GPT-6 Astra + Codex scored 2/10 after list and create pages returned HTTP 404. Source-framework wiring surviving into the target: In cargotracker-jakarta-to-spring, Gemini 3.8 Flash + mini-swe retained JSF/JoinFaces wiring in the Spring Boot target, which then failed during startup while creating a facesContext bean. Packaging incompatible with the target runtime: In cart-spring-to-jakarta, GPT-6 Astra + Codex reached a deployment failure because the packaging type left by the migration was not supported by the target Liberty runtime. These failures illustrate why ScarfBench validates beyond compilation: Nearly three in four classified failures in this evaluation appeared at runtime. Agent efficiency reveals different operating profiles On the 200 tasks remaining after the four-task sensitivity exclusion, Claude Opus 5 + Claude Code used the fewest median turns at 32. GPT-6.1 Sol + Codex used 36, Gemma 4 26B-A4B + mini-swe 40, Gemini 4 Argon + Antigravity 42, GPT-6 Astra + Codex 45, Kimi K3 + kimi-code 47, Qwen 3.8 Max + qwen-code and Gemini 3.1 Pro + OpenHands 53, Claude Opus 5.5 + Claude Code 64, and Gemini 3.8 Flash + mini-swe 79. Where harness-reported cost was available — for the Claude Code, Codex, mini-swe and kimi-code harnesses; the Antigravity, qwen-code and OpenHands harnesses did not emit per-run cost — the configurations showed distinct cost profiles: Model / harness Median turns Turns, successful runs Cost / successful run Cost per solved task Claude Opus 5 / Claude Code 32 30 $1.76 $3.83 Claude Opus 5.5 / Claude Code 64 60 $5.98 $10.10 GPT-6.1 Sol / Codex 36 34 $0.64 $1.25 GPT-6 Astra / Codex 45 44 $3.55 $6.65 Gemini 3.8 Flash / mini-swe 79 74 $0.73 $1.59 Kimi K3 / kimi-code 47 44 $1.27 $3.

title: Vibe genes? Natural(ish) language comes to protein, genome design software
abstract: Protein design tools may be getting increasingly sophisticated , but you still need a sophisticated understanding of protein structure for them to work. This can include knowing enzyme mechanisms down to the positions of specific amino acids, as well as the water molecules that also occupy the area where catalysis takes place. Once you specify these, the tools can build the rest of a protein around this target. A large collaboration of researchers based in China, however, decided to bring protein design to the masses, making a tool that can take natural language prompts and use them to produce proteins with the function you specify. If your measure for success is a working protein, then the success rate may not be great. But they still manage to get the job done. And, in a separate announcement, Hugging Face shared that it's now hosting a tool that does similar things on the DNA level. The equivalent of vibe coding may have come to protein design—at least if you have access to a lab where you can sort the good designs from the dozens of failed ones.

title: DeepMind unveils Genie 4 world model promising more realistic physics and humans
abstract: Last year, Google DeepMind sent gaming stocks tumbling with the reveal of its Genie 3 world model . Since then, world models have become a major focus of AI labs around the world, but Google isn't resting on its laurels. Researchers have been hard at work on an updated model that improves on Genie 3 in almost every way. And if you pay Google enough money, you might actually get to use Genie 4 before too long. It's easy to look at the output of Genie 4 and see a video game, which is why Genie 3 caused so much consternation in the gaming industry. DeepMind doesn't think about it that way, though. According to Google , world models are a key element in the march toward artificial general intelligence (AGI). A world model creates a virtual world, but it doesn't require pre-rendering environments or programming interactive elements. You simply tell the model what you want, and it generates the experience frame by frame in real time as you explore it. DeepMind says this technology could create infinite training environments for physical robots or unlock new avenues of rapid prototyping for creative fields. Of course, that requires the model to accurately simulate what you want. Genie 4 has several improvements that make its simulations more useful, and that's thanks in part to Google's updated Gemini models.

title: Anthropic Versus Anthropic
abstract: Anthropic is a frustrating company. Sometimes it will do things I greatly appreciate, including at substantial cost. They have taken bold stands, have a unique governance structure and have hired and worked to establish a relatively strong (but I think still inadequate) safety culture. Other times, it will do things that are deeply disappointing. It produces very good models. That too is not entirely a good thing. One can both be the best given the alternatives, and insufficient to meet the moment. Ultimately, what you think about Anthropic depends on what parts you care about most, and what you think would be sufficient. Anthropic is great if you think the problems are important and difficult, but within the range of what Anthropic’s approaches can solve. If you think we mainly need operational excellence and caring about safety and the future, then there are some non-excellent operations to fix but that goal seems doable for Anthropic. If you think the problems go well beyond that, then things look rather grim for everyone. Today’s post begins with a continuation of discussion over Anthropic’s leaked draft bill . See my previous coverage for details of the bill, which was a variation on the Frontier Act that was stronger in some ways and weaker in others, and not clearly superior to passing nothing given how much state law it would have preempted. Tomorrow’s post will cover Anthropic’s S- 1, which has now been filed with the SEC , to give me the necessary time to actually Do the Reading. Mostly. It repeats a lot. It is amazingly great that Dario Amodei responded directly , at length and with substance, to Nathan Calvin’s criticism of Anthropic’s response s on its leaked bill. I don’t agree with everything Dario said, but more like this please, from everyone. The core question Nathan Calvin asked is, what even is Anthropic? Dario counters Nathan’s list by offering a list of his own: SB 53, crazy aggressive bio filtering, delaying Mythos, the essay Policy on the AI Exponential, the clash with DoW, support of export controls (as, although he virtuously does not mention it himself, OpenAI stops supporting them), not selling to PRC-based companies, extensive reports and cards, and the recent 5% stock contribution to a public benefit fund. It is true that these came at substantial cost to Anthropic. Dario points out you could suggest ulterior motives for each decision. I don’t think any of them are ‘nefarious schemes.’ I do think in several cases Anthropic’s hand was forced by legitimate other consideration, including in ways not obvious to the public. Dario then challenges Nathan’s list a bit. Here were Nathan’s items: He says items 1-4 are ordinary business and predate the Pacing the Frontier call. He agrees 7-9 ‘could have been handled better’ and takes responsibility but seems to think that this level of performance is not obviously a mistake, as the correct rate of error is not zero. He defends the RSP changes and FCF (items 5-6) as necessary for flexibility. The bottom line argument from Dario is: Anthropic sends plenty of costly signals and makes sacrifices, and he is proud of the overall record despite some mistakes. In the interest of public record I will now include Dario’s entire reply. It is totally fine not to read it and rely on my above summary. Dario Amodei : Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin . I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safety and believe your comments are coming from a constructive, honest place, and that it benefits the public to have people whose job is to scrutinize the actions of frontier AI companies. I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic. That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it. I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits: 1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed. 2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it. 3. Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do. 4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this. 5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future. 6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent. 7.

title: How Anthropic ships Claude with Claude: Separating the Brain from the Hands
abstract: Watch the full episode on YouTube As we learned from the Anthropic S-1 filings yesterday , the lab has some of the highest revenue and research efficiency in human history, particularly with -126% loss to 19% GAAP profit turnaround in the last year. The company credits this to their two core loops: Improvement and Investment: Today we go inside how Anthropic works. Now the dust has settled on Opus 5.5 and it has lasted a month as the generally accepted #1 LLM in the world, we dive into its launch, and how Anthropic ships Claude with Claude with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang , heads of Engineering and Product respectively. The team is working under two kinds of pressure. The models are getting more capable, which makes safe deployment and access decisions harder. At the same time, usage is growing fast enough that ordinary infrastructure choices—like how much CPU an API consumes—become strategic. Those problems meet in the product choices that reach developers. Anthropic's Opus 5.5 launch emphasizes both model quality and cost. We discuss feedback that the previous Opus generations were be too verbose, alongside the need for stronger intelligence per dollar. Anthropic says the new model costs less to run than its predecessor; the exact saving depends on the workload and its use of cached context. The less visible launch work involves changes to how people integrate the API. One example we discuss is protecting model reasoning against extraction used for distillation. Preserving thinking blocks across turns helps address this, but a new requirement can also break a customer's existing harness. Katelyn also describes what being part of early access programs actually looks like in practice: Customers run evaluations in their own harnesses, report surprising behavior, and sometimes pass along less formal impressions. The useful part is not just a benchmark score: it is seeing the model in environments and tasks Anthropic's own products do not cover. As we have said for 4 straight years now on the podcast , having good evals is golden. Our favorite mental model in the episode is the distinction between an agent's brain and its hands. In Managed Agents , Anthropic separates the session log and harness from the sandbox that executes code. The harness can persist while an execution environment is created when needed; a failed sandbox does not have to take the whole agent session with it. We covered this in the Thariq pod : Claude Code’s Next Era — Thariq Shihipar, Anthropic — Latent Space Shipping Opus/Sonnet 5.5, Mods, Plugins, Projects, Tag while Pacing the Frontier The same separation gives security a useful architectural property. If generated code runs in a sandbox that never receives a service credential, there is no credential in that sandbox for the code to read. The episode describes credentials held separately and attached through a proxy, alongside controls on where sandbox traffic can go. Anthropic's containment write-up describes the wider set of isolation and network controls used across its products. The distinction matters for performance too. The guests say an earlier approach put the whole coding agent in a sandbox behind an API. Starting the environment and agent added work before the first response; if the sandbox disappeared, so did the running agent. Separating the pieces allowed the platform to pursue lower latency and better reliability while keeping execution isolated. It is a helpful lens for anyone designing an agent runtime. Ask which parts need to survive, which parts execute untrusted work, and which secrets actually need to be present where code runs. The implementation will differ between products, but those questions remain useful. Managed Agents also provides a base for experiments in memory and multi-agent workflows. Dreaming is simply implemented as one agent inspecting another agent's prior work and writing memories back. That makes the feature an example of building a higher-level behavior out of the same underlying managed-agent primitives. Their account of the roadmap is more nuanced than a list of features. Memory and learning remain important, but the team says more of its immediate attention has moved to safety as model launches have become harder. They also discuss keeping the base harness relatively simple, while letting developers experiment with verifiers, parallel agents and other strategies on top. Ideas mentioned for future platform capabilities should be treated as plans, not shipped promises. The conversation about evaluations follows naturally. A harness is an application, but improving one starts to resemble research: pick a goal, measure behavior, inspect failures, and iterate. The guests and hosts discuss using models to help build and analyze evaluations, while retaining enough judgment to decide whether the evaluation reflects a real user's job. Claude Opus 5.5 announcement — Anthropic's launch notes on model behavior, evaluation and pricing. Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang at Anthropic's partner summit — Anthropic identifies their platform engineering and product roles. Scaling Managed Agents: Decoupling the brain from the hands — The session, harness and sandbox architecture discussed in the episode. How Anthropic contains Claude across products — How Anthropic describes isolation, credentials and network controls across its products. Effective harnesses for long-running agents — Earlier Anthropic work on the challenge of maintaining progress across context windows. Anthropic model system cards — The company's public model evaluation and safety documentation. Names and wording may need correction; speaker identities have not been assigned. 0:00 Hi, today we're trying something new. We're launching coverage of Anthropic for the IPO. They just filed the S1 as of today. And so we're releasing a series of podcasts leading up to the IPO, which is expected to be in two weeks for $2 trillion. And it's one of the fastest growing companies of all time with a reported lifetime cash raise of hundreds of over $100 billion and a lifetime burn of less than $10 billion. So there are a lot of efficiency stories to dive into there, and I think that's something that we want to cover, how Anthropic is simultaneously shipping the strongest models in the world while also doing it very, very efficiently and building an incredible business. So I've pulled out, you know, a lot of you know, if you've been listening to the podcast, that I have a former life as a financial analyst. 0:50 And I pulled out some statements from the S1, which I thought would be interesting to give context to today's podcast.

title: How Anthropic ships the #1 LLM in the World safely: Separating the Brain from the Hands
abstract: Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang join Latent Space to explain the engineering behind the Claude Platform: launching Opus 5.5, separating the model’s “brain” from the agent’s “hands,” scaling APIs, and building reliable managed agents.
